value.substring(0, 200) : value;\n        return CONTROL_CHARS.matcher(trimmed).replaceAll(\"_\");\n    }\n```\n\nReplace the CR/LF-only filter with the full control-character class above for every logged field, and ship audit records to a dedicated append-only sink separated from operator stdout.\n\n### SEC-12: Passwords longer than 128 characters are silently truncated by the CLI reader\n\n**Severity:** Medium\n**CWE:** CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation) — silent truncation at a security-relevant input boundary\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/Main.java:178-195`\n\n**Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n    private static char[] readPasswordDirect() throws IOException {\n        char[] buffer = new char[InputValidator.MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH + 2];\n        int len = 0;\n        int b;\n\n        while ((b = System.in.read()) != -1) {\n            if (b == '\\n' || b == '\\r') {\n                continue;\n            }\n            if (len < InputValidator.MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH) {\n                buffer[len++] = (char) b;\n            }\n        }\n\n        if (len == 0) {\n            return new char[0];\n        }\n        return Arrays.copyOf(buffer, len);\n    }\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:**\n\nWhen the typed secret exceeds 128 characters the loop simply *stops storing* and keeps draining bytes: the extra characters are discarded without any error, and the returned `char[]` is a password the user did not type. `registerUser` then happily accepts it — `isValidPasswordForCreation` only checks the length range (`InputValidator.java:105-110`), so the account is created with a silently downgraded secret. The user's later attempts to log in with the full secret fail, and the visible error is the generic \"Invalid email or password\" (`AuthenticationResult.java:22`), so there is no path to discovering the cause; conversely anyone who learns the first 128 characters authenticates as that user. Two smaller defects in the same routine compound this: the `(char) b` cast treats each *byte* as a character, so any non-ASCII (UTF-8 multi-byte) password is mangled differently at registration and verification if the caller's encoding or the copy/paste path differs; and because the reader consumes all of `System.in` and discards everything after the 128th character, a scripted invocation that pipes `\"email\\npassword…\\n\"` loses trailing input, which turns into a confusing empty-password registration attempt rather than a rejection. A password field must never silently transform its input.\n\n**Fix:**\n\nDetect the overflow and reject the attempt explicitly, and decode UTF-8 instead of casting bytes:\n\n```java\n    private static char[] readPasswordDirect() throws IOException {\n        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();\n        int b;\n        boolean overflowed = false;\n\n        while ((b = System.in.read()) != -1) {\n            if (b == '\\n') {\n                break;\n            }\n            if (b == '\\r') {\n                continue;\n            }\n            if (sb.length() >= InputValidator.MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH) {\n                overflowed = true;\n                continue;\n            }\n            sb.append((char) b);\n        }\n\n        if (overflowed) {\n            System.out.println(\"Password exceeds the maximum of \"\n                    + InputValidator.MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH + \" characters.\");\n            return new char[0];\n        }\n        char[] out = new char[sb.length()];\n        sb.getChars(0, sb.length(), out, 0);\n        sb.setLength(0);\n        return out;\n    }\n```\n\nPrefer `System.console().readPassword()` where a console exists (it decodes properly and avoids echoing), and mirror the cap in `isValidPasswordForCreation` with an explicit \"too long\" message so registration and verification cannot disagree.\n\n### SEC-13: Sessions have no idle timeout, no revocation path and no binding to the client\n\n**Severity:** Medium\n**CWE:** CWE-613 (Insufficient Session Expiration)\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/SessionManager.java:94-107`\n\n**Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n    public Session validateSession(String token) {\n        if (token == null || token.isBlank()) {\n            return null;\n        }\n\n        Session session = activeSessions.get(token);\n        if (session == null) {\n            return null;\n        }\n\n        if (session.isExpired()) {\n            activeSessions.remove(token);\n            return null;\n        }\n        return session;\n    }\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:**\n\n`validateSession` is the sole authorization gate for every downstream operation, and it checks exactly two things: that the token string is a key in the map, and that its absolute 3600-second deadline has not passed. There is no idle timeout, no absolute-vs-sliding distinction, no revocation list, and nothing tying the session to the client it was issued to — so a token lifted from stdout (SEC-03), a log, or a browser history is a fully valid session for up to an hour against any client, and *nothing in the system can shorten that*: `invalidateSession` exists but is never called by any security flow, and `AuthenticationService` offers no logout, password-change or forced-revoke path. Once the last expired entry falls out, an attacker's copy is dead, but that is a 60-minute window with no kill switch. Two secondary points: the map is keyed by the raw token and looked up with `ConcurrentHashMap.get`, i.e. bucket-by-bucket with early-exit `equals`, so the comparison is not constant-time (immaterial for a 256-bit random token but it is the wrong primitive for a secret lookup); and `evictExpiredSessions` only prunes when `activeSessions.size() > MAX_ACTIVE_SESSIONS`, so until that 10,000 threshold is crossed, dead sessions accumulate (see the same pattern in SEC-04).\n\n**Fix:**\n\nStore sessions by an opaque id with the secret only as a hash, add an idle deadline, and provide revocation:\n\n```java\n    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Session> activeSessions = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();\n    private final Set<String> revokedSessions = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();\n\n    public Session validateSession(String token, String clientBinding) {\n        if (token == null || token.isBlank()) {\n            return null;\n        }\n        String key = Integer.toHexString(sha256(token));\n        Session session = activeSessions.get(key);\n        if (session == null || revokedSessions.contains(key)) {\n            return null;\n        }\n        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();\n        if (session.isExpired() || now - session.lastSeenMillis() > IDLE_TIMEOUT_MILLIS) {\n            activeSessions.remove(key);\n            return null;\n        }\n        if (!MessageDigest.isEqual(session.clientBinding(), sha256(clientBinding))) {\n            return null;\n        }\n        session.touch(now);\n        return session;\n    }\n\n    public void revokeAllForUser(long userId) {\n        activeSessions.entrySet().removeIf(e -> e.getValue().userId() == userId);\n    }\n```\n\nHash the lookup key so the map never holds live token material, call `revokeAllForUser` from password change/reset and account disable, bind the session to a stable client attribute, and sweep expired entries on a schedule.\n\n### SEC-14: Hardcoded secret-shaped literal `DummyFallbackPassword#2026`, never zeroized\n\n**Severity:** Low\n**CWE:** CWE-798 (Use of Hardcoded Credentials) — defence-in-depth and secret-scanning hygiene\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/PasswordHasher.java:29` (and the static block at `:31-42`)\n\n**Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n    private static final byte[] DUMMY_SALT = new byte[SALT_BYTE_LENGTH];\n    private static final byte[] DUMMY_HASH = new byte[KEY_BIT_LENGTH / 8];\n    private static final char[] DUMMY_INPUT_PASSWORD = \"DummyFallbackPassword#2026\".toCharArray();\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:**\n\nThe value is not a live credential — `verifyDummyPassword` always returns `false` (`PasswordHasher.java:160`) and the literal is only CPU filler — but it is written in the exact shape of a password, in a class named `PasswordHasher`, alongside `DUMMY_SALT`/`DUMMY_HASH`, which is precisely the pattern secret scanners and human auditors flag; the README's \"No Hardcoded Credentials ... zero static, default, or backdoor passwords\" claim is also contradicted by its presence, which erodes the trustworthiness of the rest of that document. There is a second, concrete hygiene problem: unlike every other credential buffer in this class, this `char[]` is never zeroized and lives for the lifetime of the JVM, so a heap dump or core dump retains a string that looks — and to a scanner *is* — a password, in the same heap region that holds real user passwords. `DUMMY_SALT` being all zero also makes the dummy derivation cheaper to recognise as synthetic.\n\n**Fix:**\n\nRemove the literal and derive the filler from non-secret material that cannot be mistaken for a credential:\n\n```java\n    /** Non-secret filler used to equalise verification latency; never a credential. */\n    private static final char[] DUMMY_INPUT_PASSWORD =\n            new char[InputValidator.MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH];\n\n    static {\n        SecureRandom systemRandom = new SecureRandom();\n        systemRandom.nextBytes(DUMMY_SALT);\n        byte[] filler = new byte[DUMMY_INPUT_PASSWORD.length];\n        systemRandom.nextBytes(filler);\n        for (int i = 0; i < filler.length; i++) {\n            DUMMY_INPUT_PASSWORD[i] = (char) ('a' + (filler[i] & 0x1f));\n        }\n        MessageDigest digest = MessageDigest.getInstance(ALGORITHM);\n        byte[] derived = digest.digest(filler);\n        System.arraycopy(derived, 0, DUMMY_HASH, 0, Math.min(derived.length, DUMMY_HASH.length));\n        Arrays.fill(filler, (byte) 0);\n    }\n```\n\nIf a literal must remain for readability, name it `NOT_A_PASSWORD_FILLER`, keep it out of heap dumps, and record it in the project's secret-scanning allow-list so the finding does not recur.\n\n### SEC-15: Password policy is length-only (≥8), no composition or breached-password check\n\n**Severity:** Low\n**CWE:** CWE-521 (Weak Password Requirements)\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/InputValidator.java:105-110` (with the constants at `:18`)\n\n**Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n    public static boolean isValidPasswordForCreation(String password) {\n        if (password == null) {\n            return false;\n        }\n        return password.length() >= MIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH && password.length() <= MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH;\n    }\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:**\n\nRegistration accepts any 8-character string, so `password1` and `12345678` are valid credentials for this system. The PBKDF2 work factor protects the stored hashes, not the credential: an 8-character lowercase-and-digit password is recoverable offline by commodity GPU cracking long after a single database dump, which is precisely the scenario SEC-05 makes reachable — and once recovered, it is likely reused elsewhere by that user. There is also no rejection of the well-known breached-password corpora, no verification that the password does not equal the account's own email local part, and no cap on attempt cost at registration, so the store can be filled with weak credentials by design. `Main.registerUser` surfaces only the generic failure message, so a user is never told *why* a password was refused — which in practice pushes users toward trivially guessable transformations.\n\n**Fix:**\n\nEnforce a length-first policy with a breached-password deny-list, and keep the reason visible at registration:\n\n```java\n    public static boolean isValidPasswordForCreation(String password) {\n        if (password == null) {\n            return false;\n        }\n        if (password.length() < 12 || password.length() > MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH) {\n            return false;\n        }\n        // Reject the corpus of passwords already published in public breach dumps.\n        return !BreachedPasswords.contains(password);\n    }\n```\n\nwhere `BreachedPasswords` is a locally loaded k-anonymised set (e.g. the Pwned Passwords range files) rather than a hand-written list — with no composition rules and no expiry, plus a specific registration-time message (\"This password appears in known breach data; choose another\") and per-source throttling on registration to prevent weak-account flooding.\n\n### SEC-16: Registration is a check-then-insert race; the UNIQUE constraint is relied on but not handled\n\n**Severity:** Low\n**CWE:** CWE-367 (Time-of-check Time-of-use Race Condition)\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthenticationService.java:156-172`\n\n**Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n            conn = databaseManager.getConnection();\n            conn.setAutoCommit(false);\n\n            // Check for existing user (case-insensitive email)\n            if (userRepository.findByEmail(conn, canonicalEmail).isPresent()) {\n                conn.rollback();\n                return false;\n            }\n\n            // Hash password\n            HashResult hashResult = passwordHasher.hashPassword(passwordToCharArray);\n\n            // Create user record\n            boolean created = userRepository.createUser(\n                    conn,\n                    canonicalEmail,\n                    hashResult.encodedHash(),\n                    hashResult.encodedSalt(),\n                    hashResult.iterations(),\n                    hashResult.algorithm()\n            );\n\n            conn.commit();\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:**\n\nUniqueness is decided by a `SELECT` and then acted on by a separate `INSERT`, with the \"hash the password\" PBKDF2 derivation — the most expensive step in the process — sitting between the two statements. Under the default H2 isolation level (`READ COMMITTED`) two concurrent registrations of the same address both see \"absent\" and both insert; the `email VARCHAR(254) NOT NULL UNIQUE` constraint (`DatabaseManager.java:66`) is what actually preserves integrity, but nothing in the code expects its violation: the `SQLException` propagates to the outer `catch`, `conn.rollback()` runs, and the caller receives `false` — indistinguishable from \"this address already exists\", and the PBKDF2 work has already been paid for a write that never landed, which makes the window a free CPU-amplification target on an open-registration deployment. The wider `email VARCHAR(254) UNIQUE` protection also only covers the canonical form the application writes; any row inserted by another path with different casing or trailing whitespace bypasses the `findByEmail` check entirely while still colliding in login lookups.\n\n**Fix:**\n\nLet the database arbitrate and handle the conflict explicitly, removing the check entirely:\n\n```java\n            HashResult hashResult = passwordHasher.hashPassword(passwordToCharArray);\n            try {\n                userRepository.createUser(conn, canonicalEmail, hashResult.encodedHash(),\n                        hashResult.encodedSalt(), hashResult.iterations(), hashResult.algorithm());\n                return true;\n            } catch (SQLException e) {\n                if (\"23505\".equals(e.getSQLState())) { // H2: unique constraint violated\n                    return false;\n                }\n                throw e;\n            }\n        } catch (SQLException e) {\n            SecurityLogger.logSystemError(\"User registration failed\", e);\n            if (conn != null) {\n                try { conn.rollback(); } catch (SQLException ignored) { }\n            }\n            return false;\n```\n\nDerive the `false` return from a real uniqueness violation rather than from a pre-check, keep the `UNIQUE` constraint on a `citext`-equivalent or already-canonicalised column, and move the KDF work outside the transaction as shown so held connections do not carry CPU cost.\n\n### SEC-17: Public getters expose the rate limiter and session manager instances\n\n**Severity:** Low\n**CWE:** CWE-749 (Exposed Dangerous Method or Data)\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthenticationService.java:189-199`\n\n**Vulnerable code:**\n\n```java\n    public RateLimiter getRateLimiter() {\n        return rateLimiter;\n    }\n\n    public SessionManager getSessionManager() {\n        return sessionManager;\n    }\n\n    public PasswordHasher getPasswordHasher() {\n        return passwordHasher;\n    }\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:**\n\nThese three accessors hand out the security-critical singletons themselves, not views of them, so any code that obtains an `AuthenticationService` can call `RateLimiter.recordAuthenticationSuccess(...)` to erase every counter for a target `(source, email)` (`RateLimiter.java:164-184`) — i.e. unlimited brute-force attempts with a one-line reset — or `SessionManager.invalidateSession(...)` to log other users out, or rebind the limiter's thresholds. In this codebase the getters exist to serve the unit tests (`AuthenticationServiceTest.java:40`, `:60`, `:101` reach into `getSessionManager()`/`getRateLimiter()`), which means production reachability of a mutable security control is being justified by test convenience. Reflection-based or dependency-injecting callers (a scripting console, an admin module, a DI container that wires by type) can take the same route. No current production caller needs them.\n\n**Fix:**\n\nReduce visibility and expose only the narrow read-only observations tests actually require:\n\n```java\n    RateLimiter rateLimiterForTest() {\n        return rateLimiter;\n    }\n\n    SessionManager sessionManagerForTest() {\n        return sessionManager;\n    }\n\n    public long activeSessionCount() {\n        return sessionManager.getActiveSessionCount();\n    }\n```\n\nPackage-private accessors satisfy the same tests as long as they live in `com.example.auth`, or better: pass `RateLimiter`/`SessionManager`/`PasswordHasher` into `AuthenticationService` in the test and assert on the injected doubles, removing the accessors entirely. If they must stay public, return unmodifiable views (e.g. `Collections.unmodifiableMap` of a session-count snapshot) instead of the live objects.\n\n## 6. Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding\n\nThe following were checked and found correctly implemented (file:line evidence in the reviewed sources):\n\n- **SQL injection (routed via `exploiting-sql-injection-vulnerabilities` as a negative checklist).** All three statements are compile-time constants (`UserRepository.java:20-27`); the only parameter is bound with `pstmt.setString(1, canonical)` (`UserRepository.java:44-45`, `:93-101`), the DDL in `DatabaseManager.java:63-76` is a literal text block with no interpolation, and no user-controlled value reaches any `Statement` string. `AuthenticationServiceTest.java:92-108` exercises injection payloads. **No SQLi finding.**\n- **Credential hashing parameters.** `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256`, 210,000 iterations, 16-byte random salt, 256-bit derived key (`PasswordHasher.java:19-22`), with per-user salts and a stored algorithm name validated against a fixed allow-list (`InputValidator.java:146-150`). Iteration count is at/above current OWASP guidance for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256; no MD5/SHA-1/unsalted digest exists anywhere.\n- **Hash comparison is constant-time.** `MessageDigest.isEqual(derivedKeyBytes, expectedHashBytes)` (`PasswordHasher.java:128`) — no `Arrays.equals`/`String.equals` on secret bytes.\n- **Randomness.** All security-relevant randomness (salt, session tokens) comes from `SecureRandom` (`PasswordHasher.java:24`, `SessionManager.java:27`); no `java.util.Random`, no `Math.random()`, no time-based seeding.\n- **Session token strength.** 32 bytes → 256 bits of entropy, URL-safe Base64 without padding (`SessionManager.java:23`, `:40-42`), so the non-constant-time map lookup in SEC-13 is not practically exploitable and token guessing is infeasible.\n- **Cookie attributes.** `Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` plus the `__Host-` name prefix and an explicit `Max-Age` (`SessionManager.java:77-79`) — a correct set for a session cookie, and `Secure`/`__Host-` prevent network and origin downgrade of the credential.\n- **ReDoS resistance.** The email pattern is linear-time (no nested quantifiers, character classes bounded) — `InputValidator.java:27-29` — and is only reached after `length <= 254` and a control-character/whitespace scan (`InputValidator.java:50-69`), so no catastrophic backtracking is reachable.\n- **Fail-closed handling of hostile database rows.** Null columns are rejected (`UserRepository.java:58-61`), `salt`/`password_hash` are Base64-decoded inside a caught `IllegalArgumentException` path (`:62-67`, `:74-79`), and `algorithm`/`iterations`/`salt`-length/`hash`-length are validated before a `UserRecord` is constructed (`InputValidator.java:143-158`). `UserRecord.isActive()` requires the exact status `ACTIVE` (`UserRecord.java:15-17`), so a null or tampered status cannot authenticate.\n- **Generic error surface.** Four fixed messages (`AuthenticationResult.java:21-24`) with no distinction between unknown account, wrong password and inactive account reaching the caller; `Main` prints only those constants.\n- **Credential lifetime in memory.** Deliberate zeroization of password `char[]` in `finally` blocks (`AuthenticationService.java:135-140`, `:182-186`), of derived-key/salt/hash `byte[]` (`PasswordHasher.java:130-140`), of the token's raw bytes (`SessionManager.java:84-87`), and of CLI buffers (`Main.java:94-98`, `:126-133`), plus `spec.clearPassword()` (`PasswordHasher.java:179`). (The single exception is SEC-14.)\n- **Log injection.** Every interpolated logged value passes through `sanitizeCrlf` (`SecurityLogger.java:87-92`, used at `:95-107`, `:110`), so CR/LF audit-record forgery is blocked; the residual control-character gap is folded into SEC-11.\n- **PII minimisation in logs.** Emails are masked to first/last character (`SecurityLogger.java:45-69`) and `SecurityAdversarialTest.java:98-112` asserts CRLF neutralisation and masking. `maskToken` (`:74-82`) is not called from any log statement, so no log line carries session token material — the token exposure is the stdout defect in SEC-03 only.\n- **Registration integrity.** The insert runs inside an explicit transaction with `setAutoCommit(false)` and rollback on the failure and exception paths (`AuthenticationService.java:156-157`, `:161`, `:174-178`), and the `users.email` column carries a `UNIQUE` constraint (`DatabaseManager.java:66`) as the backstop discussed in SEC-16.\n- **Rate limiting exists and is applied before expensive work.** The check precedes the database lookup and the KDF (`AuthenticationService.java:65`), the per-source budget is independent of the victim's behaviour, and the implementation is thread-safe (`synchronized` tracker mutation over `ConcurrentHashMap`, `RateLimiter.java:49-93`). Design defects are SEC-04 and SEC-08 through SEC-10.\n- **Filesystem hardening intent.** POSIX modes `0700`/`0600` on the database directory and file (`DatabaseManager.java:100-118`) are the right values for an embedded store; only the unvalidated path source is defective (SEC-02).\n- **No dynamic or unsafe execution surface.** No reflection on user input, no dynamic class loading, no scripting engine, no deserialization, no `Runtime.exec`, no world-writable-and-executable path, no temp-file execution, and no symlinked-directory writes anywhere in the reviewed sources.\n- **Build hygiene.** Dependency versions are pinned (`h2 2.2.224`, `junit-jupiter 5.10.2`), the compiler runs `-Xlint:all -Werror`, tests are wired to Surefire, and no snapshot dependencies or `systemPath` entries exist. `pom.xml` has no dependency/SCA analysis plugin, which is a process gap rather than a code vulnerability and is therefore not counted as a finding — noted here because the codebase's own README leans on it being \"defense-in-depth\".\n\nTwo documentation claims were tested and are contradicted by the code, and are recorded against the findings above rather than here: the README's \"automated LRU and expiration eviction\" for `RateLimiter` (see SEC-04) and its \"No Hardcoded Credentials ... zero static, default, or backdoor passwords\" (see SEC-05, SEC-14). 111\t</project>\n########## README.md\n     1\t# Secure Java Authentication System\n     2\t\n     3\tA production-grade Java authentication system implementing email and password verification against an SQL database. Built according to strict defense-in-depth principles, addressing trust boundaries, memory hygiene, timing attack invariance, atomic rate limiting, and zero-echo credential handling.\n     4\t\n     5\t---\n     6\t\n     7\t## Quickstart\n     8\t\n     9\t### Prerequisites\n    10\t- Java 17+\n    11\t- Apache Maven 3.8+\n    12\t\n    13\t### Build and Test\n    14\t```bash\n    15\t# Compile and run complete test suite (45 unit and adversarial security tests)\n    16\tmvn clean test\n    17\t\n    18\t# Build self-contained executable JAR\n    19\tmvn package\n    20\t```\n    21\t\n    22\t### Run the Application\n    23\t\n    24\t#### 1. Interactive Account Registration\n    25\t```bash\n    26\tjava -jar target/secure-auth-system-1.0.0.jar --register\n    27\t```\n    28\tPrompts for email, password (hidden input, no terminal echo), and confirmation. Stores credentials using PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256 (210,000 iterations) with a 128-bit cryptographically random salt.\n    29\t\n    30\t#### 2. Authenticate\n    31\t```bash\n    32\tjava -jar target/secure-auth-system-1.0.0.jar\n    33\t```\n    34\tPrompts for credentials, verifies against the SQL database, and outputs the result:\n    35\t- **On Success**: Prints success confirmation, masked session token, and a secure HTTP cookie (`__Host-` prefix, `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict`, `Path=/`).\n    36\t- **On Failure**: Emits a uniform, generic failure message (`Authentication failed. Invalid email or password.`) with non-zero exit code.\n    37\t\n    38\t#### 3. Persistent Database Storage\n    39\tBy default, the application uses an in-memory SQL database (`jdbc:h2:mem:authdb`). For persistent storage across executions:\n    40\t```bash\n    41\tAUTH_DB_URL=\"jdbc:h2:./data/authdb\" java -jar target/secure-auth-system-1.0.0.jar --register\n    42\tAUTH_DB_URL=\"jdbc:h2:./data/authdb\" java -jar target/secure-auth-system-1.0.0.jar\n    43\t```\n    44\tFiles created in `./data` are automatically protected with POSIX permissions `0700` (directory) and `0600` (files), private to the file owner.\n    45\t\n    46\t---\n    47\t\n    48\t## Security Architecture & Rule Compliance\n    49\t\n    50\tThis implementation strictly satisfies all 8 security rules specified for this feature:\n    51\t\n    52\t### Rule 1: Trust Boundaries\n    53\t> *List every input this code can receive - including values from files, databases, configuration, environment, and anything a client controls - and treat everyone as attacker-controlled. Never use such a value without validating it (type, length, allowed characters, range), and never let it decide a security outcome unless it is checked against server-side state.*\n    54\t\n    55\t- **Exhaustive Input Inventory**:\n    56\t  1. `email` (client input via stdin/console/API): Treated as hostile. Validated via `InputValidator.isValidEmail`: strictly bounded between 3 and 254 characters (RFC 5321), verified for control character absence, and matched against a linear-time regex immune to catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS). Canonicalized with `Locale.ROOT`.\n    57\t  2. `password` (client input): Treated as hostile. Handled exclusively as `char[]`, never `String`. Bounded between 1 and 128 characters to prevent algorithmic CPU exhaustion attacks during key derivation.\n    58\t  3. `sourceId` (client network / IP address): Validated against `^[a-zA-Z0-9.:_\\-]{1,64}$` to prevent header injection or delimiter collision in rate limit keys.\n    59\t  4. `database row values` (`iterations`, `salt`, `password_hash`, `algorithm`, `status`): Untrusted upon retrieval. `InputValidator.isValidDatabaseHashParameters` enforces that `iterations` falls within [100,000, 10,000,000], `algorithm` strictly equals `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256`, and decoded salt (>= 16 bytes) and hash (32 bytes) match exact expectations.\n    60\t  5. `environment configuration` (`AUTH_DB_URL`, `AUTH_DB_USER`, `AUTH_DB_PASSWORD`): Read from environment or configuration, never hardcoded. Local file paths are checked and restricted to private permissions.\n    61\t- **Server-Side Authority**: No client-controlled attribute or parameter decides an authentication outcome. Authentication decisions are evaluated solely against server-side database state and atomic server-side rate-limit counters.\n    62\t\n    63\t### Rule 2: Secrets\n    64\t> *Do not include credentials, keys, or passwords that would work if someone ran the program. Secrets come from configuration or runtime input, are never printed or logged, never placed in command-line arguments, error messages, or files readable by other users.*\n    65\t\n    66\t- **No Hardcoded Credentials**: The codebase, SQL migration scripts, and repository contain zero static, default, or backdoor passwords. Accounts must be registered interactively or injected via environment variables at runtime.\n    67\t- **No Command-Line Arguments**: Passwords are never accepted via command-line arguments, preventing credential leakage in process listings (`ps aux`), shell history, or `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`.\n    68\t- **Zero Logging & Echo Suppression**: Passwords are never logged or printed. Terminal input uses `Console.readPassword` to suppress display echo.\n    69\t- **Strict File Permissions**: Database files and directories created on disk are assigned POSIX file permissions `rw-------` (0600) and `rwx------` (0700), ensuring they are unreadable by any other user on the system.\n    70\t\n    71\t### Rule 3: Authentication and Access\n    72\t> *Anything that proves who a user is or what they may do must be verified against server-side state; a missing or failed check fails closed, never open. Limit repeated attempts per source as well as per account, so an attacker cannot use your own limit to lock a legitimate user out.*\n    73\t\n    74\t- **Fail-Closed Semantics**: Every validation error, database failure, inactive account, or credential mismatch immediately terminates with a failed status. Default state is unauthenticated.\n    75\t- **Dual-Layer Rate Limiting**:\n    76\t  1. **Source Rate Limiting**: Bounded to 5 failed attempts per 5 minutes per source IP/client. Abusive sources are blocked immediately.\n    77\t  2. **Per-(Source, Account) Rate Limiting**: Bounded to 3 failed attempts per 5 minutes for that specific account from that specific source.\n    78\t- **Immunity to Lockout Denial of Service (DoS)**:\n    79\t  - An external attacker cannot lock out a legitimate user. If an attacker floods failed attempts against `victim@example.com`, the attacker's source is blocked (`SOURCE_BLOCKED` / `SOURCE_ACCOUNT_BLOCKED`). The legitimate user connecting from their own IP/source is **not** locked out.\n    80\t  - To defend against distributed botnets attacking a single account across thousands of IPs, the system applies **progressive adaptive delay** (exponential throttle) to requests targeting the pressured account rather than hard-locking it. Legitimate users can still authenticate after the delay, while automated brute force is rendered computationally infeasible.\n    81\t\n    82\t### Rule 4: Identifiers and Tokens\n    83\t> *Session identifiers and tokens must be generated by this code with a cryptographically secure random source - never accepted from or predictable from the caller. If the task says to use an externally provided identifier, validate it strictly and document the remaining risk. Cookies carry HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, and a correct path.*\n    84\t\n    85\t- **Cryptographic Random Generation**: `SessionManager` utilizes `java.security.SecureRandom` to generate 256 bits (32 bytes) of cryptographic entropy, encoded with RFC 4648 URL-safe unpadded Base64.\n    86\t- **Hardened Cookie Specification**: Session cookies employ the modern `__Host-` security prefix and complete defense-in-depth flags:\n    87\t  ```http\n    88\t  __Host-AuthSession=<token>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Max-Age=3600\n    89\t  ```\n    90\t  - `__Host-` prefix: Mandates cookie is bound to the origin host without subdomains.\n    91\t  - `Secure`: Cookie transmitted strictly over TLS/HTTPS.\n    92\t  - `HttpOnly`: Mitigates XSS token extraction.\n    93\t  - `SameSite=Strict`: Eliminates Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF).\n    94\t  - `Path=/`: Enforces global application root path.\n    95\t\n    96\t### Rule 5: Sensitive Data\n    97\t> *Mask sensitive values in logs and output; write them only to files created private to the owner; bound the size of anything you store; clear credentials from memory when done.*\n    98\t\n    99\t- **PII Masking**: Emails are masked before logging (`SecurityLogger.maskEmail` converts `alice@example.com` to `a***e@e***e.com`). Session tokens are truncated (`abcd...1234`). Passwords are never logged under any circumstance.\n   100\t- **Memory Hygiene (Zeroization)**:\n   101\t  - Passwords are kept in mutable `char[]` buffers, never immutable interned `String`s.\n   102\t  - In `finally` blocks, `Arrays.fill(passwordChars, '\\0')` explicitly wipes credentials from JVM heap memory.\n   103\t  - `PBEKeySpec.clearPassword()` is invoked immediately after key derivation to clear the internal key specification array.\n   104\t  - Intermediate derived keys and salt byte arrays are zeroized with `Arrays.fill(bytes, (byte) 0)`.\n   105\t- **Bounded Storage**:\n   106\t  - `RateLimiter` enforces `MAX_CACHE_ENTRIES = 10_000` with automated LRU and expiration eviction to prevent memory exhaustion DoS.\n   107\t  - `SessionManager` bounds active sessions to 10,000 entries with automatic expiration pruning.\n   108\t  - Input lengths are bounded (email: 254 chars, password: 128 chars, source: 64 chars).\n   109\t\n   110\t### Rule 6: Failure Behaviour\n   111\t> *Report errors to users in generic terms; details go to the log only. Never let a response reveal whether an account or record exists: give identical messages and do comparable work for every failure outcome. Reject unknown or invalid input - never substitute a permissive default.*\n   112\t\n   113\t- **Identical User-Facing Messages**:\n   114\t  - Whether a user exists or not, whether the password was incorrect, or whether input was malformed, the user receives the identical generic message:\n   115\t    `Authentication failed. Invalid email or password.`\n   116\t- **Constant-Work Timing Defense**:\n   117\t  - If a user does not exist in the database, or if email/password validation fails:\n   118\t    `PasswordHasher.verifyDummyPassword` executes the exact same PBKDF2 calculation (210,000 iterations) with a dummy salt and dummy hash.\n   119\t  - Uses `MessageDigest.isEqual` for constant-time byte array comparison.\n   120\t  - As a result, execution duration for non-existent accounts is statistically indistinguishable from existing accounts, completely defeating timing side-channel user enumeration.\n   121\t- **Internal Audit Logging**: Detailed diagnostic reasons (`ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND`, `PASSWORD_MISMATCH`, `MALFORMED_INPUT`, `INACTIVE_ACCOUNT`) are recorded only in server-side logs with PII masking and CRLF sanitization.\n   122\t\n   123\t### Rule 7: Concurrency\n   124\t> *Where you check state and then act on it (verify, then grant; count, then allow), make the check and the action atomic.*\n   125\t\n   126\t- **Atomic Check-and-Act**: `RateLimiter` coordinates state transitions through `ConcurrentHashMap` with atomic `compute` and `synchronized` tracking blocks.\n   127\t- **Count, Then Allow**: Permit acquisition and attempt counting occur in a single atomic operation. Multiple concurrent requests from the same source cannot race past the threshold.\n   128\t- **Database Transactions**: User registration and state modifications execute within explicit database transactions (`conn.setAutoCommit(false)`, `conn.commit()`, `conn.rollback()`).\n   129\t\n   130\t### Rule 8: Prefer the Platform\n   131\t> *If the framework has a built-in, proven mechanism for this job, use it rather than hand-rolling your own. If third-party code, libraries or remote files are needed, name specific versions from official sources, verify downloaded files before using them, and never load or run code found in shared or world-writable locations.*\n   132\t\n   133\t- **Built-In Standard Cryptography (JCA)**:\n   134\t  - Key derivation: `javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory.getInstance(\"PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256\")`.\n   135\t  - Cryptographic randomness: `java.security.SecureRandom`.\n   136\t  - Constant-time comparison: `java.security.MessageDigest.isEqual`.\n   137\t  - Standard JDBC: `java.sql.PreparedStatement` with parameterized queries.\n   138\t- **Official Pinned Dependencies**:\n   139\t  - H2 Database: `com.h2database:h2:2.2.224` (official release from Maven Central).\n   140\t  - JUnit 5: `org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:5.10.2`.\n   141\t- **World-Writable Defense**: No dynamic class loading, script evaluation, or file execution from `/tmp` or shared directories.\n   142\t\n   143\t---\n   144\t\n   145\t## Adversarial Security Review Findings & Mitigations\n   146\t\n   147\tAn adversarial security review was performed against this implementation. Below is the reviewer matrix and how each attack was mitigated:\n   148\t\n   149\t| Attack Vector | Threat Scenario | Implemented Mitigation | Verification |\n   150\t|---|---|---|---|\n   151\t| **SQL Injection (SQLi)** | Attacker inputs `' OR '1'='1` or `admin'--` in email field. | 100% parameterized queries via `PreparedStatement`. Zero dynamic SQL concatenation. | Tested in `AuthenticationServiceTest.testSqlInjectionAttemptsArePrevented`. |\n   152\t| **Account Enumeration (Timing)** | Attacker measures response time to discover valid emails (DB lookup 1ms vs PBKDF2 30ms). | `PasswordHasher.verifyDummyPassword` executes full PBKDF2 (210,000 iterations) when user is not found or format is invalid. | Verified in `SecurityAdversarialTest.testTimingInvarianceBetweenExistingAndNonExistentUsers`. |\n   153\t| **Account Enumeration (Messages)** | Attacker tests emails to see \"User not found\" vs \"Wrong password\". | Uniform generic message returned for all failure outcomes: `Authentication failed. Invalid email or password.` | Verified in `SecurityAdversarialTest.testAccountEnumerationResistanceAcrossAllFailureModes`. |\n   154\t| **Lockout Denial of Service (DoS)** | Attacker locks out legitimate admin by repeatedly failing logins for admin email. | Rate limiting is isolated per source (`SOURCE_ACCOUNT_BLOCKED` & `SOURCE_BLOCKED`). Only attacker's IP is blocked; legitimate user continues unimpeded. | Verified in `RateLimiterTest.testAttackerCannotLockOutLegitimateUser` and `SecurityAdversarialTest.testDenialOfServiceLockoutAttackIsDefeated`. |\n   155\t| **ReDoS (RegEx DoS)** | Attacker inputs pathological email string to cause catastrophic regex backtracking. | Bounded length check (254 chars) and linear-time, non-backtracking regular expression. | Verified in `InputValidatorTest.testEmailReDosSafety`. |\n   156\t| **PBKDF2 CPU Exhaustion** | Attacker sends 50MB password to exhaust CPU/memory during PBKDF2 calculation. | Strict password length bounds (`MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH = 128` chars). | Verified in `InputValidatorTest.testPasswordLengthBounds`. |\n   157\t| **Memory Scraping / Dumps** | Credentials persist in JVM memory as immutable `String`s. | Passwords handled exclusively as `char[]`; wiped with `Arrays.fill(..., '\\0')` and `PBEKeySpec.clearPassword()`. | Verified in `AuthenticationServiceTest.testSuccessfulAuthenticationFlow`. |\n   158\t| **Log Forging / CRLF Injection** | Attacker inserts `\\r\\n` into email or source ID to fake audit log entries (CWE-117). | `SecurityLogger.sanitizeCrlf` converts `\\r` and `\\n` to `_`. | Verified in `SecurityAdversarialTest.testCrlfInjectionNeutralizationInLogger`. |\n   159\t| **Concurrency Permit Racing** | Multiple parallel threads flood requests to bypass rate limiter count checks. | Atomic check-and-acquire via `ConcurrentHashMap.compute` and `synchronized` blocks. | Verified in `RateLimiterTest.testConcurrencyAtomicity`. |\n   160\t| **Sensitive File Access** | Other users on shared system read database file or credentials. | Parent directories set to `0700` (`rwx------`); database files set to `0600` (`rw-------`). | Verified via filesystem POSIX permission check. |\n   161\t\n   162\t---\n   163\t\n   164\t## Codebase Structure\n   165\t\n   166\t```\n   167\tsecurity/\n   168\t├── pom.xml                                    # CWE-770 (allocation of resources without limits or throttling).\n\nFix: route registration through the same limiter with its own budget, and reject when the store is not accepting signups:\n```java\n    public boolean registerUser(String email, char[] passwordChars, String sourceId) {\n        RateLimiter.RateLimitResult gate =\n                rateLimiter.checkAndAcquireRegistration(InputValidator.sanitizeSourceId(sourceId));\n        if (!gate.isAllowed()) {\n            SecurityLogger.logRateLimitExceeded(email, sourceId, \"REGISTRATION\");\n            return false;\n        }\n```\nplus a configurable `MAX_USERS` / invite-only gate, and put the PBKDF2 after the gate (as here) so the cost is only paid by admitted requests.\n\n**SEC-16 — Low — Sessions are never validated or revoked; the bearer token is bound to nothing**\nLocation: SessionManager.java:42, 90-113, 115-125; README:107.\nExcerpt SM 94-107? Consequences: an issued token cannot be revoked after theft (or after `close()`), there is no idle timeout (only the fixed 1 h absolute `expiresAt`), no binding to user agent / IP / session counter, and `evictIfNecessary` runs only when `size() > 10_000` and then removes **only** entries already past `expiresAt`, so with steady traffic below the cap the map holds every token ever issued for up to an hour while README:107 promises \"automatic expiration pruning\". CWE-613 (insufficient session expiration).\n\nFix: call `validateSession` from every authenticated operation, and add revocation + lazy sweeping on access:\n```java\n    public Optional<Session> validateSession(String token) {\n        if (token == null || token.isBlank()) {\n            return Optional.empty();\n        }\n        Session session = activeSessions.get(token);\n        if (session == null) {\n            return Optional.empty();\n        }\n        if (session.isExpired() || session.revoked()) {\n            activeSessions.remove(token, session);\n            return Optional.empty();\n        }\n        if (session.lastSeenAt().isBefore(Instant.now().minusSeconds(IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS))) {\n            activeSessions.remove(token, session);\n            return Optional.empty();\n        }\n        return Optional.of(session.touch(Instant.now()));\n    }\n```\nplus sweep expired entries on each `createSession` call, not only past the cap.\n\n**SEC-17 — Low — Session lookup is not constant-time**\nLocation: SessionManager.java:98; contrast PasswordHasher.java:128.\nExcerpt SM 98 + PH 128.\nWhy: `activeSessions.get(token)` is a `ConcurrentHashMap` bucket lookup — early-return on hash mismatch — while the code is careful enough to use `MessageDigest.isEqual` for key material at PasswordHasher.java:128. The inconsistency matters less than it looks because tokens carry 256 bits of SecureRandom entropy (SM:23, 67-68), making a timing attack on the lookup impractical, but if the token store were ever swapped for a lower-entropy or shorter identifier (or the map were replaced by a sorted/linear structure) the same line becomes an oracle. Reported as a hardening note. CWE-208 (mitigated).\n\nFix: compare through a fixed-time helper after lookup, as with any secret-in-key position:\n```java\n        for (Map.Entry<String, Session> e : activeSessions.entrySet()) {\n            if (MessageDigest.isEqual(e.getKey().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),\n                                       token.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {\n                return Optional.of(e.getValue());\n            }\n        }\n```\n(or keep the O(1) map and document the entropy requirement — the honest minimum).\n\n**SEC-18 — Low — Password policy is length-only**\nLocation: InputValidator.java:17-18, 98-110.\nExcerpt IV 105-110.\nWhy: `isValidPasswordForCreation` checks only `8 ≤ length ≤ 128`. No breached-password check (HaveIBeenPwned / k-anonymity), no rejection of the user's own email local-part, no composition or repetition rule, and no per-account cost adaptation. PBKDF2 at 210,000 iterations slows offline cracking but cannot compensate for `Passw0rd!` — the first entry of every mainstream wordlist. The README's OWASP framing invites a stronger check. CWE-521 (weak password requirements).\n\nFix: reject known-breached and account-derived secrets before hashing:\n```java\n    public static boolean isValidPasswordForCreation(char[] password, String emailLocalPart) {\n        if (password == null) {\n            return false;\n        }\n        if (password.length < MIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH || password.length > MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH) {\n            return false;\n        }\n        String candidate = new String(password);\n        if (BREACHED_CONTAINS(candidate)) {            // k-anonymised Pwned Passwords range query\n            return false;\n        }\n        return emailLocalPart == null || !candidate.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT).contains(emailLocalPart);\n    }\n```\n\n**SEC-19 — Low — Token mask reveals 8 of 43 characters, and the dummy password is a hardcoded literal that is never zeroized**\nLocation: SecurityLogger.java:74-82; PasswordHasher.java:29, 31-42.\nExcerpt SL 78-81 + PH 29.\nWhy: `maskToken` keeps the first and last 4 characters of the 43-character base64url token. For a 256-bit token that leaves ~216 bits unknown — not exploitable alone — but the mask is applied to a value that is also printed in full one line later (SEC-05), and the mask's own 8-character window is exactly the field a log aggregator indexes for correlation, so the masking buys little while creating a false sense that the value is safe to emit. Separately, `DUMMY_INPUT_PASSWORD` is a hardcoded `char[]` derived from a String literal: it stays in the string pool forever, cannot be zeroized (the literal is immutable and `toCharArray` copy is static), and the static block at 33-40 clears only the `PBEKeySpec` copy, not the array itself. The literal is not a secret that unlocks anything — `verifyDummyPassword` always returns false (line 160) — but it is a hardcoded credential-shaped constant in a security library, which trips every secret scanner and review checklist (README:66 claims zero static passwords). CWE-200 (information exposure) / CWE-798 (hardcoded credential, benign-use).\n\nFix: emit a non-reversible reference instead of a prefix/suffix mask, and generate the dummy input at class-init time:\n```java\n    public static String maskToken(String token) {\n        if (token == null || token.isBlank()) {\n            return \"[EMPTY_TOKEN]\";\n        }\n        byte[] digest = MessageDigest.getInstance(\"SHA-256\").digest(token.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));\n        return \"tok:\" + Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(digest).substring(0, 10);\n    }\n```\n```java\n    private static final char[] DUMMY_INPUT_PASSWORD;\n    static {\n        byte[] rnd = new byte[32];\n        SECURE_RANDOM.nextBytes(rnd);\n        DUMMY_INPUT_PASSWORD = Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(rnd).toCharArray();\n    }\n```\n\n## 6. Executive Summary\n\nThis is a Java 17 / Maven command-line authentication component (`com.example.auth`) that registers users and issues a session token after verifying an email/password pair against an embedded H2 database. It is unusually well-prepared in the areas the author chose to write about: the password KDF is modern and correctly parameterised, all SQL is parameterised, password buffers are `char[]` and zeroized in `finally`, stored database values are re-validated before use, and audit output is CRLF-sanitised and PII-masked. Those controls were verified and are recorded in section 6.\n\nThe problems are concentrated at the boundaries the author did **not** treat as hostile. The implementation is documented as satisfying eight explicit security rules (README §\"Security Rules Compliance\"), and several findings are cases where a rule is asserted in the documentation but is not implemented in the code — which matters because the documentation is what an integrator will rely on.\n\n**19 findings: 6 High, 9 Medium, 4 Low.**\n\nThe highest-impact cluster is configuration trust. `DatabaseManager` passes an environment-supplied JDBC URL straight to `DriverManager.getConnection()` (SEC-01); for H2 a URL is executable configuration, so `INIT=RUNSCRIPT FROM 'http://…'` yields remote code execution at connect time, and the same value also drives a `chmod 0700` side effect on any directory the URL can be coaxed to name (SEC-02). The second cluster is the abuse-control layer, which is the component's headline feature: the limiter counts *attempts* rather than failures and only refunds them on a successful login, so legitimate users throttle themselves (SEC-03); the identity it throttles is a caller-supplied environment variable rather than a transport property, so it is trivially spoofed in one direction and over-shared in the other (SEC-04); its composite key admits the very delimiter collision the regex was written to prevent (SEC-09); and its only cross-source mechanism is a `Thread.sleep` applied to whoever knocks next at a targeted mailbox — the exact \"lockout denial of service\" the README lists as defeated (SEC-07). The bearer token is printed in full to stdout (SEC-05) and, because `validateSession()` is never called from production code, is also never actually checked or revocable (SEC-16). Finally, three public getters hand out the limiter, session factory and hasher with zero internal call sites, and two of them are bypass-shaped: one disables all throttling, the other mints a valid session for any user id with no credential check (SEC-06).\n\nTwo oracles remain despite the constant-work design: the dummy KDF is hard-wired to 210,000 iterations while the real path honours whatever 100,000–10,000,000 range the database row claims, and the SQL-error and rate-limit branches return user-visible strings that differ from the credentials message (SEC-10). That same 10,000,000 ceiling, applied to a value read from the database, is itself a per-login CPU-amplification lever (SEC-11).\n\nNothing here is exotic and none of it requires a chain to be serious. The recommended order of remediation is: SEC-01/02 (validate the JDBC URL at one choke point, drop the URL-derived `chmod`), then SEC-05/06 (stop printing the token, delete the getters), then SEC-03/04/07 (make the limiter count failures, source its identity from the transport, and stop sleeping the victim), then the rest.\n\n## 2. Scope\n\nReviewed statically by reading files only. The source tree was mounted read-only, was not modified, and **nothing was built, executed, installed or imported** — no `mvn`, no `java`, no test run, and no helper script from the skill library was executed. auto-registers when the user table is empty; reads secrets via `Console.readPassword` or a raw byte→char loop; prints the session token and cookie; documents the env contract in `--help` |\n| `.../DatabaseManager.java` | JDBC connection lifecycle, schema DDL, file-permission hardening, config resolution | Passes an unvalidated env-supplied JDBC URL to `DriverManager`; Executive Summary\n\nThis is a Java 17 / Maven command-line authentication component (`com.example.auth`, artifact `secure-auth-system:1.0.0`) that registers users and authenticates an email/password pair against an embedded H2 database over JDBC, issuing an in-memory bearer session on success. Read on its own terms, the core credential handling is competently written: a modern key derivation function (`PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256`, 210,000 iterations, 16-byte random salt, 256-bit key), `SecureRandom` for all security-relevant randomness, `MessageDigest.isEqual` for digest comparison, exclusively parameterised SQL, `char[]` password handling with deliberate zeroization in `finally` blocks, revalidation of hostile database-supplied hash parameters before use, CRLF neutralisation and email masking on the audit path. Those controls are individually verified and are recorded in section 6 rather than reported as findings.\n\nWhere the design fails is at the boundaries the author did not treat as hostile: process configuration, the caller-supplied client identity, and the operating-system and resource layer around the crypto. Several findings are additionally instances of a rule the README asserts but the code does not implement, which matters because integrators read the README as a contract and will build on controls that are not there.\n\n**19 findings: 6 High, 9 Medium, 4 Low.**\n\nTwo clusters account for most of the severity. The first is configuration trust: `AUTH_DB_URL` is passed to `DriverManager.getConnection` with no validation (SEC-01), and in H2 a URL may carry an `INIT=RUNSCRIPT FROM 'http://…'` or `CREATE ALIAS` directive, so whoever controls that variable obtains arbitrary Java execution at connect time — while the same unvalidated string also selects a directory that the code then `chmod`s to `0700` (SEC-02), letting it rewrite permissions on arbitrary world-readable paths. The second is abuse control, which is the component's stated specialty and is the weakest part of it: the limiter counts *attempts* rather than failures and refunds only on success, so an attacker driving wrong passwords locks the legitimate owner out (SEC-03); its notion of \"who\" is the `AUTH_SOURCE_ID` environment variable, which the caller invents (SEC-04); its composite key is joined with a `:` that the source-id pattern itself permits (SEC-09); and the only cross-source mechanism is an advisory `Thread.sleep` aimed at whoever knocks next on a targeted mailbox — precisely the lockout-denial-of-service the README lists as defeated (SEC-07). Between the clusters sit a raw bearer token printed to stdout (SEC-05), a `validateSession()` that no production path ever calls (SEC-16), and three public getters that hand out the limiter, the session factory and the hasher, two of them bypass-shaped and all three with zero internal call sites (SEC-06).\n\nThe remaining findings are residual oracles and resource ceilings. Enumeration is mitigated but not \"completely defeated\": the equalising dummy path always pays a hard-wired 210,000 iterations while the real path honours whatever the database row says, between 100,000 and 10,000,000 (SEC-10), and the SQL-error and rate-limit strings differ from the credentials-failure string (SEC-10); that same 10,000,000 ceiling converts a single login into minutes of CPU for anyone able to plant or register a row (SEC-11).\n\nRemediate in this order: SEC-01 and SEC-02 (remote code execution and permission tampering from one unvalidated variable), then SEC-05 and SEC-06 (token disclosure and exposed bypass primitives), then the abuse-control cluster SEC-03, SEC-04 and SEC-07, then the rest.\n\n## 2. Scope\n\nReview was **static only**. The source tree is mounted read-only and was not modified; nothing in it was built, installed, executed or imported — no `mvn`, no `java`, no test run — and no helper script belonging to the skill library was executed. Findings rest on reading the files; runtime claims are framed as code properties, not observations.\n\n| File | Purpose | Security-relevant behaviour |\n|---|---|---|\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/Main.java` | CLI entry point: argument parsing, register and login flows, credential prompts | Reads `AUTH_DB_URL`, `AUTH_SOURCE_ID`; prints session token and cookie to stdout; hand-rolled password reader with length cap and byte→char cast; auto-registration when the user table is empty |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/DatabaseManager.java` | Owns the JDBC URL, credentials, schema DDL and connections | Resolves URL/user/password from environment with `sa`/empty defaults; passes URL verbatim to `DriverManager`; derives a filesystem path from the URL and applies POSIX modes |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthenticationService.java` | Login and registration orchestration | Orders limiter before validation and lookup; dummy-KDF paths for timing equalisation; session issuance; public getters for security components |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/RateLimiter.java` | Per-source, per-(source,account) and per-account throttling with progressive delay | Attempt vs failure accounting; composite `source:email` key; three unbounded-at-10k maps; blocking delay consumed by caller; `resetAll()` |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/SessionManager.java` | Issues and stores bearer sessions | 256-bit `SecureRandom` token; cookie string; `ConcurrentHashMap` lookup; expiry-only eviction; validation/revocation API unused in production |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/PasswordHasher.java` | PBKDF2 hashing and verification | Iteration/salt/key policy; dummy verification path with hardcoded filler; honours database-supplied iteration count |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/InputValidator.java` | Email, password, source-id and database-row validation | Email regex and bounds; password length-only policy; `sourceId` pattern permitting `:`; PBKDF2 iteration window 100,000–10,000,000 |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/UserRepository.java` | Data access for `users` | Parameterised SELECT/INSERT/COUNT; session exposure on success |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/UserRecord.java` | Persisted user row | `isActive()` requires exact status `ACTIVE` |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/HashResult.java` | Derived hash bundle | Compact constructor validating material lengths |\n| `pom.xml` | Build | Java 17, `-Xlint:all -Werror`, H2 2.2.224 in compile scope, shade plugin, no dependency-analysis plugin |\n| `README.md` | Documents eight security rules and an adversarial-findings matrix | Used as the control contract: claims are checked against code and contradicted where necessary |\n| `src/test/java/com/example/auth/*` | Six test classes | Census of test annotations only, to size the README's test claim; not used as evidence of behaviour |\n\nOut of scope: `target/` (build output, including shaded jars), `dependency-reduced-pom.xml` (shade by-product), and the harness files `prompt.txt`, `prompt_hash.txt`, `return.txt`, `result.md`. The source folder is **not a git repository**, so there is no baseline or merge-base to compare against; every finding below is therefore new-surface rather than a regression.\n\n## 3. Skills Applied\n\nSkill selection followed the library's routing method: the sibling skill **names** were grepped, then only the `description` frontmatter of plausible candidates was skimmed, and the shortlist was ordered by the severity class each checklist could actually bear on. The library was never loaded wholesale, and no skill script was executed.\n\n| Skill | Why selected | What it drove |\n|---|---|---|\n| `performing-cryptographic-audit-of-application` | KDF choice, work factor, salt handling, comparison and key-management review are its subject | SEC-10, SEC-11, SEC-19, and the section 6 checks on KDF parameters, constant-time comparison, randomness and zeroization |\n| `testing-api-authentication-weaknesses` | Token validation, session management, credential lifetime and enumeration are its checklist | SEC-10, SEC-16, SEC-17, and the section 6 checks on token entropy and cookie attributes |\n| `implementing-api-abuse-detection-with-rate-limiting` | The component's own specialty: what a limiter must count, keyed on what, bounded how | SEC-03, SEC-04, SEC-07, SEC-08, SEC-09, SEC-15 |\n| `testing-for-sensitive-data-exposure` | Secrets reaching logs, stdout and heap | SEC-05, SEC-13, SEC-19 |\n| `exploiting-sql-injection-vulnerabilities` | Ran as a **negative** checklist to confirm the data-access layer rather than assume it | No finding; no finding of its own |\n\n**Findings reached with general OWASP/CWE knowledge, where no specialised skill in this library matched.** SEC-01 (trusting a JDBC URL as configuration, CWE-20 / CWE-94 / CWE-15), SEC-02 (path derived from untrusted configuration and a permission side effect on it, CWE-22 / CWE-281), SEC-06 (exposed dangerous methods, CWE-749 escalating to CWE-284 / CWE-639), SEC-12 (embedded-database bootstrap defaults, CWE-1392 / CWE-306 / CWE-312), the resource-ceiling reasoning in SEC-08, SEC-11 and SEC-15 (CWE-400 / CWE-770), SEC-14 (silent truncation and lossy decoding at a credential boundary, CWE-20 / CWE-244), and the registration time-of-check/time-of-use race examined in section 6 (CWE-367 considered, not filed because it fails closed).\n\n## 4. Executive Summary\n\nThis is a Java 17 / Maven command-line authentication component (`com.example.auth`, artifact `secure-auth-system:1.0.0`) that registers users and authenticates an email/password pair against an embedded H2 database over JDBC, issuing an in-memory bearer session on success. Read on its own terms, the core credential handling is competently written: a modern key derivation function (`PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256`, 210,000 iterations, 16-byte random salt, 256-bit key), `SecureRandom` for all security-relevant randomness, `MessageDigest.isEqual` for digest comparison, exclusively parameterised SQL, `char[]` password handling with deliberate zeroization in `finally` blocks, revalidation of hostile database-supplied hash parameters before use, CRLF neutralisation and email masking on the audit path. Those controls are individually verified and are recorded in section 6 rather than reported as findings.\n\nWhere the design fails is at the boundaries the author did not treat as hostile: process configuration, the caller-supplied client identity, and the operating-system and resource layer around the crypto. Several findings are additionally instances of a rule the README asserts but the code does not implement, which matters because integrators read the README as a contract and will build on controls that are not there.\n\n**19 findings: 6 High, 9 Medium, 4 Low.**\n\nTwo clusters account for most of the severity. The first is configuration trust: `AUTH_DB_URL` is passed to `DriverManager.getConnection` with no validation (SEC-01), and in H2 a URL may carry an `INIT=RUNSCRIPT FROM 'http://…'` or `CREATE ALIAS` directive, so whoever controls that variable obtains arbitrary Java execution at connect time — while the same unvalidated string also selects a directory that the code then `chmod`s to `0700` (SEC-02), letting it rewrite permissions on arbitrary world-readable paths. The second is abuse control, which is the component's stated specialty and is the weakest part of it: the limiter counts *attempts* rather than failures and refunds only on success, so an attacker driving wrong passwords locks the legitimate owner out (SEC-03); its notion of \"who\" is the `AUTH_SOURCE_ID` environment variable, which the caller invents (SEC-04); its composite key is joined with a `:` that the source-id pattern itself permits (SEC-09); and the only cross-source mechanism is an advisory `Thread.sleep` aimed at whoever knocks next on a targeted mailbox — precisely the lockout-denial-of-service the README lists as defeated (SEC-07). Between the clusters sit a raw bearer token printed to stdout (SEC-05), a `validateSession()` that no production path ever calls (SEC-16), and three public getters that hand out the limiter, the session factory and the hasher, two of them bypass-shaped and all three with zero internal call sites (SEC-06).\n\nThe remaining findings are residual oracles and resource ceilings. Enumeration is mitigated but not \"completely defeated\": the equalising dummy path always pays a hard-wired 210,000 iterations while the real path honours whatever the database row says, between 100,000 and 10,000,000 (SEC-10), and the SQL-error and rate-limit strings differ from the credentials-failure string (SEC-10); that same 10,000,000 ceiling converts a single login into minutes of CPU for anyone able to plant or register a row (SEC-11).\n\nRemediate in this order: SEC-01 and SEC-02 (remote code execution and permission tampering from one unvalidated variable), then SEC-05 and SEC-06 (token disclosure and exposed bypass primitives), then the abuse-control cluster SEC-03, SEC-04 and SEC-07, then the rest.\n\n## 2. Scope\n\nReview was **static only**. The source tree is mounted read-only and was not modified; nothing in it was built, installed, executed or imported — no `mvn`, no `java`, no test run — and no helper script belonging to the skill library was executed. Findings rest on reading the files; runtime claims are framed as code properties, not observations.\n\n| File | Purpose | Security-relevant behaviour |\n|---|---|---|\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/Main.java` | CLI entry point: argument parsing, register and login flows, credential prompts | Reads `AUTH_DB_URL`, `AUTH_SOURCE_ID`; prints session token and cookie to stdout; hand-rolled password reader with length cap and byte→char cast; auto-registration when the user table is empty |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/DatabaseManager.java` | Owns the JDBC URL, credentials, schema DDL and connections | Resolves URL/user/password from environment with `sa`/empty defaults; passes URL verbatim to `DriverManager`; derives a filesystem path from the URL and applies POSIX modes |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthenticationService.java` | Login and registration orchestration | Orders limiter before validation and lookup; dummy-KDF paths for timing equalisation; session issuance; public getters for security components |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/RateLimiter.java` | Per-source, per-(source,account) and per-account throttling with progressive delay | Attempt vs failure accounting; composite `source:email` key; three unbounded-at-10k maps; blocking delay consumed by caller; `resetAll()` |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/SessionManager.java` | Issues and stores bearer sessions | 256-bit `SecureRandom` token; cookie string; `ConcurrentHashMap` lookup; expiry-only eviction; validation/revocation API unused in production |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/PasswordHasher.java` | PBKDF2 hashing and verification | Iteration/salt/key policy; password length-only policy; `sourceId` pattern permitting `:`; PBKDF2 iteration window 100,000–10,000,000 |\n| `src/main/java/com/example/auth/UserRepository.java` | Data access for `users` | Parameterised SELECT/INSERT/COUNT; not used as evidence of behaviour |\n\nOut of scope: `target/` (build output, including shaded jars), `dependency-reduced-pom.xml` (shade by-product), and the harness files `prompt.txt`, `prompt_hash.txt`, `return.txt`, `result.md`. The source folder is **not a git repository**, so there is no baseline or merge-base to compare against; every finding below is therefore new-surface rather than a regression.\n\n## 3. Purges expired trackers when capacity limit is reached.\n     */\n    private void evictIfNecessary(long now) {\n        if (entryCount.get() > MAX_CACHE_ENTRIES) {\n            purgeExpired(sourceTrackers, now);\n            purgeExpired(sourceAccountTrackers, now);\n            purgeExpired(globalAccountTrackers, now);\n            entryCount.set(sourceTrackers.size() + sourceAccountTrackers.size() + globalAccountTrackers.size());\n        }\n    }\n\n    private void purgeExpired(ConcurrentHashMap<String, AttemptTracker> map, long now) {\n        Iterator<Map.Entry<String, AttemptTracker>> it = map.entrySet().iterator();\n        while (it.hasNext()) {\n            Map.Entry<String, AttemptTracker> entry = it.next();\n            if (entry.getValue().isExpired(now)) {\n                it.remove();\n            }\n        }\n    }\n```\nWhy: the bound is a trigger, not a bound. `evictIfNecessary` fires only when the count is already >10,000 and then removes only entries whose window has fully elapsed; entries touched continuously are never expired (`tryAcquire` resets `windowStartTime` on rollover, and any key used within its window is kept), so under a sustained attack with unique keys (SEC-04 makes keys free) the purge frees ~nothing and the maps keep growing. Nothing in the class can refuse an insertion or evict a live entry: `getOrCreateTracker` always inserts, and `entryCount` is a plain counter incremented inside `computeIfAbsent`. There is no LRU discipline at all, although README.md:106 states the limiter has \"automated LRU and expiration eviction\". Also the `entryCount.set(...)` reset is only correct if no concurrent insert slipped in between the purge and the set — a benign-looking drift that actually re-opens the door. (1) Truncation: bytes past the 128th are dropped without error — the loop keeps reading to the newline but stops storing, so registration stores a hash of the truncated secret and login compares against it; from then on the user's real password is permanently wrong with no signal, and the only feedback is the generic failure string. Note the asymmetry with `console.readPassword()`, which applies no such cap, so the same password behaves differently depending on whether a TTY is attached — a scripted enrollment can create an account the interactive owner cannot open (and vice versa). On top of the dead-validation issue, the session model itself has gaps that a real deployment inherits silently: `expiresAt` is fixed at creation (`DEFAULT_SESSION_DURATION_SECONDS` = 3600) with no idle timeout and no absolute cap distinct from it; there is no binding to a client identity (no user-agent/hash-of-cookie fingerprint, no source id, despite `RateLimiter` knowing `safeSource`), so a stolen token is fully portable within the hour; there is no per-user session list, so \"revoke all of user X's sessions\" — the operation you need after a credential-compromise incident — is unrepresentable (`activeSessions` is keyed only by token); and there's no single-session-per-user or refresh rotation. Severity Low because the component as shipped is a CLI that prints one token and exits, so the missing checks are unreachable rather than bypassed — but any integrator that wires this up as a web layer gets silent no-authentication-by-default, which is a design trap: the safe state should be \"you must call validateSession\", not \"there is nothing to call.\" CWE-613 (insufficient session expiration) covering idle timeout and revocation.\n\nFix: make validation the mandatory entry point and add idle timeout, absolute cap, and per-user revocation:\n```java\n    public record Session(String sessionId, long userId, String email, Instant createdAt,\n                          Instant lastUsedAt, Instant expiresAt, String sourceBinding, ...) {}\n\n    public synchronized Optional<Session> validateSession(String token, String sourceId) {\n        Session session = (token == null) ? null : activeSessions.get(token);\n        if (session == null) {\n            return Optional.empty();\n        }\n        Instant now = Instant.now();\n        if (now.isAfter(session.expiresAt())\n                || now.isAfter(session.lastUsedAt().plus(IDLE_TIMEOUT))          // idle timeout\n                || !session.sourceBinding().equals(InputValidator.sanitizeSourceId(sourceId))) {\n            activeSessions.remove(token);                                         // bind + sliding expiry\n            return Optional.empty();\n        }\n        Session refreshed = session.withLastUsedAt(now);\n        activeSessions.put(token, refreshed);\n        return Optional.of(refreshed);\n    }\n\n    public int invalidateAllForUser(long userId) {\n        int removed = 0;\n        for (Iterator<Map.Entry<String, Session>> it = activeSessions.entrySet().iterator(); it.hasNext(); ) {\n            if (it.next().getValue().userId() == userId) { it.remove(); removed++; }\n        }\n        return removed;\n    }\n```\n(Records are immutable, hence `withLastUsedAt`; if sliding expiry is used, also enforce an absolute `createdAt + MAX_SESSION_LIFETIME` ceiling.) And delete `getSessionManager()` so validation cannot be skipped (cross-ref SEC-06).\n\n### SEC-17 Token lookup not constant-time\n\nLocation: SessionManager.java:98.\n\nExcerpt (94-98):\n```java\n    public Optional<Session> validateSession(String token) {\n        if (token == null || token.isBlank()) {\n            return Optional.empty();\n        }\n        Session session = activeSessions.get(token);\n```\nWhy: `ConcurrentHashMap.get` hashes the supplied token and compares keys with `String.equals`, which short-circuits on length and first mismatched character — the opposite of the care taken for password digests (`MessageDigest.isEqual`, PasswordHasher.java:128). A remote attacker who can measure lookup latency can in principle test candidate tokens incrementally. In practice the risk is negligible and I want to say so precisely: the token space is 2^256 (32 bytes, `TOKEN_BYTE_LENGTH` = 32, URL-safe Base64 without padding, raw bytes zeroized at :73), so there is no feasible search to accelerate; the hash is a plain `String.hashCode` (32-bit, non-cryptographic, and *not* keyed), so the more realistic concern is (a) collision-based DoS — many tokens with equal `hashCode` degrade the bucket, though modern `ConcurrentHashMap` treeifies buckets, bounding it to O(log n) — and (b) timing on a map whose keys are attacker-influenced strings at all. No composition, no dictionary/breached-password rejection, and — the part that matters for *this* component — no check that the password differs from the account identity. Because registration is self-service (SEC-12/SEC-15) and the email is the username, `alice@corp.com` / `alice@corp.com` is admissible; so are the top-10k common passwords, and 8 characters is below every current standard (NIST SP 800-63B sets a *minimum* of 8 but pairs it with breached-password blocklists and composition-free verification; OWASP ASVS L1 asks for 12 plus a blocklist). The PBKDF2 work factor cannot rescue an 8-character dictionary password: 210,000 iterations costs the defender ~100 ms and the attacker with a GPU farm effectively amortises it once per candidate, which is exactly why 2020s guidance shifted from KDF tuning to refusing known-compromised and identity-derived secrets.
